text:
I really enjoyed catching some of your streams over the last few months. I appreciate the attitude of "wonder" and "let's see what we can do" with these tools. I respect the honesty of admitting not knowing how to code, and it was genuinely cool to see how that is no longer a barrier to building tech. I also respect that you started learning.

With that said, I have watched as you've figured out the game of social media - drama, click baiting, etc. This, I was sorry to see, but I stuck around.

Many people have a lot to say about Theo. He has strong opinions, not always correct (as with any of us), but the one thing that is clear to anyone who has been in this space is that he does understand the difficult pieces of software devekopment and much of the CS field overall. This understanding is at a level very few ever get to.

When he offered to have an independent auditor check both, you met it with "he's just jealous."

Building cool stuff with vibe coding is great, but this is like asserting you can build a better pharmaceutical with a few prompts and no real knowledge of the field than someone with the background, who also uses the same tools.

Some humble advice, for what it is worth: I'd love to see you return to the honesty about what you don't know and take challenges with grace and as an opportunity to learn more and get better at what you do.

Attention gained by cheap tricks like drama and clickbait _feel_ free, but they aren't. They chip away at your reputation, and that is something that is very hard to ever regain. Once it's gone, it often stays gone. When all is said and done, you've traded your birthright for a bowl of beans.

This is said with a genuine hope for a bright future for you. You have a lot of road ahead, and you're sharp enough to do some very cool things. Hopefully you won't let the easy roads distract you from what you could do.

text:
Three rural Irish comedies by John McDwyer offer audiences an evening of sharp dialogue, unexpected twists, and characters who feel recognisably local rather than stage Irish. 

The Pension Plan centres on the bachelor Flanagan brothers, content on their hillside farm until a persistent neighbour and a visiting stranger threaten their settled life; expect madcap plotting and a guaranteed night of laughter that still leaves room for the price of easy solutions. 

Unforgiven, first staged in 2006, follows brothers waiting on their father’s death for very different reasons while a neighbour remains unaware of the plans being made for her; a returning brother from America sets the cats among the pigeons in a rapid succession of surprises and one-liners drawn from ordinary rural life. 

Turning Mammy, described by the author as a comedy with a few serious bits, tracks two sisters and their bachelor neighbour: one searching for a child given up at birth, the other waiting for a bed-bound mother to die so a long courtship can begin. Secrets surface, motives prove less simple than they appear, and the humour sits alongside genuine melancholy.

John McDwyer was born in Sooey, County Sligo, in 1947 and has lived most of his adult life in County Leitrim. After thirty-two years with AIB he co-founded Beezneez Theatre Company in 1997 and served as its artistic director through roughly forty tours until he stepped back from the road in 2024. 

His first radio play won an RTÉ award in 1992; later stage works, including the Leitrim Trilogy, have been taken up by amateur companies across Ireland and further afield. 

Directors and actors have noted the depth he gives ordinary people without reducing them to caricature. His plays continue to be licensed for performance, with recent outings of The Pension Plan at venues such as Hawk’s Well Theatre in Sligo and regional houses on the amateur circuit. He lists The Showgrounds among his favourite places.

The plane was flying from Bermuda to Boston, and the disappearance has triggered a search by air and sea in the waters off Nantucket.: “Heartbeat 104 medevac New York Center. Good evening radar contact level 240. Roger, you said you're coming in belonging. Is that what you said? OK, you declare an emergency or no? ”
Air traffic control audio posted by https://t.co/iK0dqU6sNj offered a glimpse of the flight’s final communications. The pilot’s transmission could not be heard in the recording. The controller later confirmed the pilot was declaring an emergency just before losing contact with the plane.
The Canadian-registered air ambulance jet had four crew members and two passengers aboard when it departed Bermuda’s L.F. Wade International Airport overnight for the flight to Massachusetts.

In all of this, President Donald John Trump has violated the Article II, Section 1, Clause 8-mandated presidential oath of office to faithfully execute the office of President of the United States, and to the best of his ability, preserve, protect, and defend the Constitution of the United States; has abused the powers of the presidency by committing high crimes and misdemeanors, in a manner contrary to his trust as President; has detrimentally flouted the United States Constitution by operating vicious, quota-driven, unaccountable paramilitary forces 75 killing people (including Renée Good, Alex Pretti, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero); and is now even closer to brazenly and wantonly devolving the United States democratic republic into an authoritarian regime, where, if left in office, unjustified killings of people and coverups by ICE and CBP are normalized to the great prejudice of the cause of law and justice, and to the manifest injury of the people of the United States.

Wherefore, Donald John Trump, by such conduct, warrants impeachment and trial, and removal from office.”

DEMOCRATS NEED STRATEGY FOR STRUGGLE, NOT PARLIAMENTARY CRETINISM

On Thursday, December 11, 2025, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Democratic Whip Katherine Clark and Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar issued the following statement:
“Impeachment is a sacred constitutional vehicle designed to hold a corrupt executive accountable for abuse of power, breaking the law and violating the public trust. The effort traditionally requires a comprehensive investigative process, the collection and review of thousands of documents, an exacting scrutiny of the facts, the examination of dozens of key witnesses, Congressional hearings, sustained public organizing and the marshaling of the forces of democracy to build a broad national consensus. None of that serious work has been done, with the Republican majority focused solely on rubber stamping Donald Trump’s extreme agenda. Accordingly, we will be voting “present” on today’s motion to table the impeachment resolution as we continue our fight to make life more affordable for everyday Americans.”

This approach to the vital impeachment question might have been adequate for times of greater tranquility than our own, but this overly cautious, slow, and fundamentally timid strategy is wholly inadequate for the present acute crisis, when decisive action is required. Most obviously, the House leadership appears oblivious to the grievous damage being done by Trump and his gang to the United States and the free world, day by day, hour by hour. American citizens have been wantonly gunned down by ICE raids which have not stopped. The illegal abolition of USAID humanitarian assistance has already caused hundreds of thousands of deaths in less-developed countries, particularly in Africa, and this death toll is likely to rise into the millions unless USAID is quickly restored for the purposes directed by Congress. The pursuit of an early victory in the Iran war is being prevented by Trump’s ineffective, weak, and vacillating misleadership. Ukrainians are needlessly dying because of Trump’s vindictive refusal to provide necessary weaponry which the United States could supply without damaging our homeland defense. Most of all, one shudders to think of the dangerous and unstable combination of defeatist appeasement and enraged flight forward adventurism that might characterize Trump’s behavior in an actual strategic crisis of the type Putin and Xi are capable of triggering at any moment. Under these circumstances, it is simply not realistic to carry out the lengthy and time-consuming set piece preparations envisioned by the House Democratic leaders. They must urgently develop an emergency plan for impeachment. If Democratic Party gains in the upcoming midterms are as large as the polls suggest they will be, the need for laborious preparations to help create a consensus for impeachment will become largely irrelevant.

REP. MASSIE (R-KY): IMPEACH HEGSETH RESOLUTION

What follows is a condensed version of Congressmen Massie’s resolution; as always, the full texts of impeachment resolutions should be available on the website of the relevant House sponsor.

Impeaching Peter Brian Hegseth, Secretary of Defense, for high crimes and misdemeanors.

Resolved, That Peter Brian Hegseth, Secretary of Defense, also referred to as Secretary of War by the Administration, is impeached for high crimes and misdemeanors and that the following articles of impeachment be exhibited to the United States Senate: Articles of impeachment exhibited by the House of Representatives of the United States of America in the name of itself and of the people of the United States of America, against Peter Brian Hegseth, Secretary of Defense, in maintenance and support of its impeachment against him for high crimes and misdemeanors.

ARTICLE I: WAGING WAR IN CONTRAVENTION OF THE WAR POWERS RESOLUTION OF 1973 SECTION 2(c)
in ARTICLE II: WAGING WAR IN CONTRAVENTION OF THE WAR POWERS RESOLUTION OF 1973 SECTION 5(c)
ARTICLE III: WAGING WAR IN CONTRAVENTION OF THE WAR POWERS RESOLUTION OF 1973 SECTION 5(b)
ARTICLE IV: IGNORING LAWS THAT MINIMIZE CIVILIAN CASUALTIES
ARTICLE V: EXTRAJUDICIAL KILLINGS
ARTICLE VI: SUPPRESSING FREE SPEECH
ARTICLE VII: KIDNAPPING OF A SOVERIGN FOREIGN LEADER
ARTICLE VIII: UNLAWFUL WAR IN YEMEN

Congressmen Massie’s bill of impeachment against Hegseth is useful first of all because it shows the breadth of hostility to MAGA misrule, even among Republicans. Secondly, it provides another useful warning that all articles of impeachment are not equal. Some have merit, and some do not. Some are even dangerous. Since articles of impeachment are voted on individually, and one at a time, it is important to distinguish between articles with meritorious policy consequences on the one hand, and weak or confused articles which lead in the wrong direction, on the other. With these latter, successful passage may create very dangerous legal precedents or present an image of weakness to aggressive foreign enemies like the CRINKs. But fortunately, the passage of a single article of impeachment is all it takes to put a lawless President, cabinet officer, or any other federal official on trial in the Senate. One article is all it takes!

In Massie’s bill of impeachment, Article VI in defense of free speech is clearly meritorious and should be passed, thus putting the wrecker Hegseth into the Senate dock.  This is obviously the article which should be approved.  The articles that rely on the Vietnam era War Powers Act are by contrast very weak because of the dubious constitutionality of this law, which has never survived review in the Supreme Court. The War Powers Act can be seen as attempting to wrongly resolve an ambiguity which the framers of the Constitution showed they expressly wanted kept open by making the president the commander-in-chief of the military forces, while at the same time specifying that only Congress can declare war. The question of which should prevail in any given situation is left open. Sometimes the silences of the Constitution can have an exceptional importance. The same considerations apply to the issue of whether a war in Yemen is legal or not. Laws aimed at reducing civilian casualties are probably unenforceable, and violate the time-tested wisdom that a war cannot be run by a committee, much less by an entire house of Congress. Extrajudicial killings of alleged drug dealers are likely in the same category. Foreign sovereign leaders can have no automatic immunity for acts committed against the United States. In short, Congressmen Massie’s articles reflect to a considerable degree a Republican or libertarian-isolationist and antigovernment mentality.  He should have referred an article of impeachment identifying Hegseth as trampling on the Constitution by failing to provide for the common defense -- as government is commanded to do in the Preamble -- by his firing on various transparent pretexts of some twenty-seven flag officers regarded as potentially anti-Trump, thus doing grievous long-term damage to the US officer corps.

Get ready to vote: early in person voting or an absentee ballot deposited directly into a state drop box are best, with the latter recommended those who might face ICE harrassment. If possible avoid USPS, whose bosses are pro-Trump. In person voting on election day can be viewed as a last resort, especially in red states.

text:
OUR VOTE IS WORTH MORE THAN $5,000

GACETA MIGRANTE / Tonatiuh Cuazitl

Donald Trump has just put a number on the electoral table: $5,000.

The condition is political: a Republican victory in the House of Representatives and the Senate.

The election is close. Just a handful of districts could determine who controls the House.

This is where we come in.

The United States is approaching the midterm elections with tens of millions of Hispanic citizens eligible to vote. But one state deserves particular attention:

Texas.

Pew Research Center estimates that 6.7 million Hispanics are eligible to vote in Texas.

That is roughly 32 out of every 100 eligible voters in the state. Texas has the second-largest Hispanic electorate in the United States, behind only California.

And in Texas, the word Hispanic carries a particular historical weight.

Mexicans have long constituted, by far, the largest component of the state’s Latino electorate. In Pew’s detailed analysis of the Hispanic electorate in Texas, 87% were of Mexican origin. We are not applying that older percentage to today’s electorate to manufacture a current Mexican-American figure. It does, however, tell us which community has historically formed the backbone of Latino political power in Texas.

Now look at the 2026 electoral map.

UnidosUS identifies five Texas congressional districts among its battlegrounds with a significant Latino presence:

TX-15, TX-23, TX-28, TX-34 and TX-35.

Four of the districts in its current database alone account for more than 1.19 million registered Latino voters:

TX-15: 308,803
TX-28: 354,623
TX-34: 305,766
TX-35: 229,175

Look at TX-34.

305,766 registered Latino voters.

The Republican margin cited by UnidosUS for that contest is just 20,435 votes.

The registered Latino electorate is almost 15 times that margin.

That does not mean 305,766 people will vote for the same party.

They won’t.

It means a fraction of that electorate has enough political weight to alter the outcome of a competitive election.

The polling is also showing movement.

In May, UnidosUS surveyed 500 registered Latino voters in Texas, including a specific sample from battleground congressional districts.

77% said they were certain or almost certain to vote in November.

Among those who voted for Donald Trump in 2024, 20% said they would no longer vote for him today.

Texas.
Houston.
Ronaldo Salgado’s vote counts.

His father, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old Mexican man, left for work on July 7.

He never came home.

An ICE agent shot him during an immigration enforcement operation.

That gives the $5,000 a different meaning.

Washington can offer a dividend.

In Texas, a community of 6.7 million eligible Hispanic voters can put its own questions on the table.

Who answers for Lorenzo?

Who holds ICE accountable?

Who will require agents to be identifiable, body cameras to be used, use-of-force protocols to be public, and independent investigations when someone dies during a federal operation?

Who is willing to take those demands to Congress?

This is not about telling a Mexican American to vote Republican.

Nor Democrat.

It is about understanding the value of our vote before giving it away.

When a community represents nearly one-third of the Texas electorate, when hundreds of thousands of its voters are concentrated in contested districts, and when control of the House can depend on only a handful of seats, that community ceases to be a statistic.

It becomes political power.

Trump has put his number on the table:

$5,000.

Texas has another:

6.7 million.

And Lorenzo Salgado Araujo leaves us with the question no dividend can buy:

What is it worth to have our fathers come home alive?

Lorenzo can no longer vote.

Ronaldo can.

And so can millions like him.

OUR VOTE IS WORTH MORE THAN $5,000

We are not an audience — we are a community.

I hope your mother is doing better, but your info is not correct. I have seen interviews with the family whose grandmother was killed against (grandmother's and family) will. I have also seen an interview with one of the women who received treatment down here. Here you go:

Kristin Logan, a dual U.S.–Canadian citizen in B.C., was diagnosed with stage 4 ovarian cancer in 2023. She says a MAID pamphlet arrived before she had even seen an oncologist, after months of waiting. She and her husband say they were told treatment, including HIPEC surgery, would not save her. She went to Seattle for chemo and surgery, later moved to Texas, and is still alive after doctors in Canada said she would not last two years. 

Brigitte Stegemann, 83, died by MAID on July 10, 2026, at a care home in Cannifton, Ontario, after a stage 4 stomach cancer diagnosis. Her granddaughter, who held power of attorney, says Stegemann had refused MAID, tore out an IV port while saying “I don’t want the death shot,” failed to understand the assessment, and later cried that she had “made a mistake.” The family says she gave no clear consent the morning she died. Belleville Police are investigating. Practitioners maintain she legally consented. No charges or coroner’s finding have been reported.

Allison Ducluzeau, Victoria, B.C. In late 2022 she was diagnosed with stage 4 peritoneal carcinomatosis. She told Global News in November 2023 that a B.C. surgeon said she was inoperable, that chemotherapy would buy little time, and that she was offered MAID — twice, by her account. She found surgeons who do debulking surgery plus heated intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC). In early 2023 she was treated by Dr. Armando Sardi at Mercy Medical Center in Baltimore, at a reported cost of more than $200,000, partly raised online. She later said she felt “100 per cent,” was cycling, golfing, and running, and described a complete remission. B.C. Cancer told her the U.S. treatment “would not have been the recommended treatment” for her diagnosis and did not reimburse her. She has said she would rather have had the surgery in Canada.

Jennifer Brady, Halifax. After a 2019 hysterectomy for cervical cancer she developed severe lymphedema. Surgical options were not available to her in Nova Scotia. She spent years seeking out-of-province care, was denied coverage, and was approved for MAID. CBC reported she applied because she was in chronic pain, depressed, and spending hours a day managing swelling. A Nova Scotia court later called the denial of coverage unreasonable. The province then paid for treatment. On July 16, 2025 she had a lymph-node transplant at The Valley Hospital in Paramus, New Jersey. She said she could see her kneecaps for the first time in years, no longer needed a machine that kept her on the couch for six hours a day, and took her MAID application off the table. Her surgeon has said the operation does not cure the underlying disease.

text:
A whole Black community gave up the biggest Sunday of their year, brand new Easter clothes and all, just to keep their money out of stores that would not serve them. Within weeks the most powerful merchants in Nashville were begging them to come back, and the lunch counters opened.

The snow was still falling on February 27, 1960, when groups of young white men walked into the downtown stores and started pulling Black students off the lunch counter stools.

The students had been warned that morning. A white minister who supported them had called to say the police planned to stand aside on purpose and let them be hurt.

More than three hundred of them went downtown anyway.

They filled every stool at the counters and every seat around them, sitting in their good coats, some of them reading magazines just to keep their hands and their faces calm.

Then the men came in behind them.

They dragged the students to the floor. They kicked them, spat on them, poured mustard and ketchup over their heads, and pressed lit cigarettes into their backs and down into their hair.

A Fisk student named Paul LaPrad, one of the few white students in the movement, was singled out at the McLellan's counter after he would not answer to a slur. A man dragged him off the stool and beat him on the floor while LaPrad folded himself into the tight, head-covering crouch they had practiced for exactly this moment.

He did not swing back. Not once.

A young woman named Maxine Walker sat a few feet away and watched it happen, with no way to reach him.

When it was finally over, LaPrad picked himself up off the floor, bloody, and sat back down on the stool.

A news camera caught all of it, and the country watched it on television that night.

Then the Nashville police walked in. They arrested around eighty of the students for disorderly conduct, and they did not lay a hand on a single one of the men who had beaten them.

The attackers stood on the sidewalk and cheered as the paddy wagon filled.

And because the city jail was still segregated, LaPrad and the few other white students were locked in a separate cell, apart from the Black classmates they had just bled beside.

These were mostly kids. Students from Fisk, from Tennessee A&I, from Meharry, from American Baptist Theological Seminary.

They had spent the winter in a church basement with a young divinity student named James Lawson, learning the hardest discipline there is, how to take a beating without giving one back.

They had started sitting at the downtown counters on February 13, about a hundred and twenty-four of them, asking to be served, being refused, and sitting anyway until the stores closed. They had even run quiet test runs the fall before, going in to buy a few small things and measure how deep the hatred ran.

So they knew what they were walking into.

What they also knew, and what almost no one tells you about Nashville, is that the men who ran those stores had already confessed the one thing that would ever move them.

Months earlier, Black ministers had gone to two of the biggest store owners downtown, Fred Harvey and John Sloan, and asked them plainly to just serve Black customers at the counters. Both men said no. They said serving Black people would cost them more business than it would ever win them.

They had said it out loud themselves. It was about money.

So after the beatings, after the arrests, after the students chose jail over paying the fines, after the city offered to split the counters into a Black side and a white side and the students threw that insult right back, the movement reached for the one weapon the merchants had already admitted they feared.

Black Nashville closed its wallet.

The timing was not gentle. It was Easter.

For Black families in 1960, Easter was not a small thing. It was the Sunday of the whole year, the one morning when even families who had almost nothing put their children in brand new clothes and walked them into church with their heads held high.

The downtown stores counted on exactly that. Those few weeks were the richest stretch of their entire year.

And that spring, Black Nashville simply did not come.

They did not buy the Easter dresses. They did not buy the little suits and the Sunday shoes, and they walked their children past the bright store windows on the way somewhere else and did not go in.

Diane Nash, a twenty-two-year-old from Chicago who had become one of the movement's leaders, later said that around ninety-eight percent of Black Nashville stayed out of those stores.

Sit with what that discipline cost, quietly, in a thousand homes. A mother finding the words to tell a child there would be no new dress this year. A family letting go of the one small pride they scraped and saved all year to afford.

They gave up their Easter so that their grandchildren would not have to give up their dignity.

At the richest hour of the retail year, the cash registers downtown fell silent.

The merchants who had decided Black customers were not worth the trouble now stood in half-empty stores and learned exactly what those customers had been worth all along.

Nash put it flatly years later. The men who would not even talk to them the first time were suddenly very eager to sit down and make a deal.

For a while, the money did the work the beatings could not. And then someone decided to answer it with dynamite.

Before dawn on April 19, the city was asleep when someone crept up to the North Nashville home of Z. Alexander Looby and rolled a bundle of dynamite against the front of the house.

Looby was the attorney defending the arrested students, all hundred and fifty-three of them. He had come to America from Antigua as an orphaned fifteen-year-old and put himself through Howard, Columbia, and NYU before winning a seat on the Nashville city council.

The blast tore the entire front off his house.

It was powerful enough to blow out around a hundred and forty windows across the street at Meharry Medical College.

Looby and his wife Grafta were asleep in a bedroom at the back of the house. That single fact, which side of the house they slept on, is the only reason this is a story about a bombing and not a double funeral.

Someone had just tried to assassinate a sitting elected official over the right to order a sandwich. No one was ever arrested for it.

When a reporter reached Looby that day, he refused to give the city's fear the satisfaction it wanted. He called the bombers a hoodlum element, called it an isolated act, and said he only hoped there would be no more violence.

The people who set that bomb believed it would frighten the movement off the streets.

Instead it put the entire movement into the streets.

By early that afternoon, around three thousand people were walking down Jefferson Street toward the courthouse, and they were doing it in complete silence.

Students from all four of the city's Black colleges filled the line. At the very front walked C. T. Vivian, Diane Nash, and Bernard Lafayette, with Curtis Murphy, Kenneth Frazier, Rodney Powell, and James Lawson close behind them.

They did not chant a single word. Three thousand people moving through downtown without making a sound was heavier than any shouting could have been.

Mayor Ben West came out to meet them on the courthouse steps. One of the ministers and the mayor started sliding into a political back-and-forth, and Diane Nash stepped forward and cut it off with one question.

She asked him whether he felt it was wrong to discriminate against a person for no reason but their race or their color.

West could have hidden behind policy the way politicians always do. Instead he stopped, and he said yes, he believed it was wrong.

He explained himself later, in words that would cost him with his own white voters. He said it was a moral question, one a man had to answer as a man and not as a mayor, and that he could not defend selling a person goods in one part of his store and refusing them a meal in another.

The next morning the newspaper ran it across the front page in heavy type. Integrate Counters, Mayor.

On May 10, 1960, six downtown Nashville stores served Black customers at their lunch counters for the first time in the city's history.

The registers started ringing again. This time they rang for everybody.

Nashville became one of the first cities in the entire South to open its counters, and Dr. King later called the movement there the best organized and most disciplined in the region.

The historical marker that stands in Nashville today says the quiet part in stone. It credits the victory to two forces set side by side, the outrage over the bombing and the economic boycott.

We remember the students at the counter, and we should. They took the blows and kept their hands open, and they earned every inch of that memory.

But the thing that actually broke Nashville was quieter than a sit-in and almost impossible to fit inside a photograph.

It was thousands of people whose names were never written down anywhere, who gave up their Easter and kept their money in their pockets until the most powerful men in the city came asking them to please come back.

The maids. The schoolteachers. The day laborers. The grandmothers who walked their grandchildren past those store windows in last year's clothes and kept on walking.

There is no marker anywhere with their names on it.

So the next time you sit down at a counter in this country and no one asks what color you are before they serve you, understand that thousands of forgotten people bought that seat for you, one skipped Easter at a time.

The least their great-grandchildren are owed is to be told it was them.

Lower individual income-tax rates. The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act reduced several tax brackets and nearly doubled the standard deduction, lowering federal income taxes for many households. Many provisions were made permanent in 2025. https://t.co/HpqUul314E

Lower corporate taxes. The 2017 law reduced the federal corporate income-tax rate from 35% to 21%, increasing the money companies could retain for investment, hiring, or shareholder returns. https://t.co/HpqUul314E

Larger child tax credit. Trump’s first tax law increased the maximum credit from $1,000 to $2,000 per qualifying child; the 2025 law increased it to $2,200, subject to eligibility requirements. https://t.co/HpqUul314E

Tax relief for tipped workers. Eligible workers can deduct up to $25,000 in qualified tips annually for 2025–2028. Income limits apply, and payroll taxes still apply.

Internal Revenue Service
Tax relief on overtime. Eligible workers can deduct qualifying overtime premiums up to $12,500 annually, or $25,000 for joint filers, for 2025–2028. This generally covers the extra half of “time-and-a-half,” rather than all overtime wages. Internal Revenue Service

Additional deduction for seniors. Eligible people age 65 or older can deduct an additional $6,000 each for 2025–2028, with income phaseouts. This can reduce taxes on retirement income, although it does not repeal the tax on Social Security benefits. Internal Revenue Service

Car-loan interest deduction. Eligible buyers can deduct up to $10,000 annually in qualifying interest on loans for new vehicles assembled in the United States, for 2025–2028. Income and other restrictions apply.

Internal Revenue Service
Faster write-offs for business investment. The 2025 law restored 100% bonus depreciation for qualifying equipment and other property, helping businesses recover investment costs sooner. Internal Revenue Service

Immediate deductions for domestic research. Businesses can again deduct eligible U.S. research and experimental expenses immediately, improving cash flow for innovation. Internal Revenue Service

Investment incentives for distressed communities. Opportunity Zones provide tax incentives for investment in designated low-income areas. The program was created in 2017 and made permanent, with changes, in 2025. Its benefits vary by community. Internal Revenue Service

Children’s investment accounts. The 2025 law created Trump Accounts, including a $1,000 federal contribution for eligible U.S.-citizen children born during 2025–2028. Families must make the required election to receive that contribution. Internal Revenue Service

More assistance with adoption costs. Beginning in 2025, up to $5,000 of the adoption tax credit became refundable, helping eligible families who otherwise owe too little income tax to use the full credit. Internal Revenue Service

Very low unemployment before COVID. Unemployment reached 3.5% in 2019, its lowest level since 1969. This occurred during Trump’s presidency, building on an economic expansion that began before he took office. https://t.co/hxadEjSiCL

Higher household income and lower poverty before COVID. Census reported that inflation-adjusted median household income rose 6.8% in 2019 and the official poverty rate fell to 10.5%. These were national gains during his first term; presidential policy was one of several influences. https://t.co/KkigFFpcx7

The USMCA trade agreement. Trump negotiated and signed the replacement for NAFTA, introducing updated digital-trade rules, stronger labor enforcement, revised automotive rules, and additional agricultural market access. Congress also helped shape the final agreement.

United States Trade Representative
Renewed LNG export approvals. His second administration lifted the pause on reviewing certain liquefied-natural-gas export applications and issued approvals supporting additional American energy-export projects. Benefits include construction, supplier work, and future export earnings. Department of Energy

Major factories and infrastructure: operating, under construction, or expanding:
These projects can benefit American workers and suppliers. Credit is shared among companies, federal administrations, Congress, and state and local governments where projects span several years.

TSMC semiconductor manufacturing in Arizona — operating and under construction. The original Arizona investment was announced in Trump’s first term. Micron memory-chip expansion — construction underway. Its announced total subsequently exceeded $250 billion through 2035. Projects include Idaho factories, New York construction, and Virginia modernization. The original Idaho and New York projects began under Biden; Trump’s administration supported their expansion. Micron Technology

Apple’s American manufacturing program — partly operating, further expansion planned. Apple announced a $600 billion, four-year U.S. spending commitment. Its Houston manufacturing center opened in August 2026, supporting advanced AI-server production. Other work includes domestic chips and components. The $600 billion includes broader spending and is not entirely new factory construction. Apple

Apple-supported Colorado chip production — expansion announced. A 2026 agreement supports Broadcom’s $1.5 billion expansion and modernization in Fort Collins, adding domestic semiconductor capacity. This is included within Apple’s broader commitment. Apple

Stargate AI infrastructure — operating and under development. Announced at the White House in January 2025 with a $500 billion investment goal, Stargate includes an operating Abilene, Texas, site and other sites under development. Potential benefits include construction, computing capacity, supplier contracts, and technical jobs. The White House

Hyundai’s American expansion — projects underway and planned. Hyundai’s $26 billion commitment through 2028 includes a roughly $5.8 billion Louisiana steel mill. Additional announced business investments

IBM: $150 billion over five years for American growth and manufacturing.

text:
Not to mention it's a federal crime. Don't believe a word from this orange ass clown. It's a federal crime to attempt to buy votes. 

 Grok's answer.
      I'll check the relevant federal and state rules on paying people for their votes.

Yes. Offering money—or anything of value—in exchange for someone’s vote is illegal under federal law, and state laws generally ban it as well.

The main federal statute is 18 U.S.C. § 597. It makes it a crime to make or offer an “expenditure” to any person to get them to vote, withhold a vote, or vote for or against a candidate. It also criminalizes soliciting, accepting, or receiving such a payment in exchange for a vote. A conviction can bring a fine and up to one year in prison, or up to two years if the violation is willful.

A second federal provision, 52 U.S.C. § 10307(c), applies to elections that include federal offices (president, Senate, House, and related contests). It prohibits knowingly and willfully paying, offering to pay, or accepting payment for registering to vote or for voting. Penalties can include a fine of up to $10,000 and up to five years in prison. Election officials treat even small incentives—cash, goods, event tickets, and similar items of value—as covered “payment.”

Both the person who offers the compensation and the person who accepts it can be charged. The deal does not have to be completed; the offer or the agreement can be enough.

States have their own bans. West Virginia, for example, makes offering money or anything of value for a vote a felony. The details vary, but the basic prohibition is widespread.

Courts draw a line between this and ordinary politics. A private, targeted payment to an identifiable person for their vote (“retail” vote buying) is illegal. Broad campaign promises of general public benefits if elected (“wholesale” appeals) are generally treated as protected political speech, not vote buying (see *Brown v. Hartlage*, 1982). Paying people for campaign work that is not conditioned on how they vote is also different from buying the vote itself.

This is an interesting way of thinking about why the denial of Jewish peoplehood fits so comfortably into contemporary leftwing politics. I’d add another dimension to it.

The denial of Jewish peoplehood on the left actually has a very long ideological and political history & is intimately tied to the history of leftwing antizionism. In my lectures, I trace it back to the early 20th century, when the Bolsheviks were arguing with Zionists over the solution to the “Jewish Question.”

The idea of Jewish peoplehood wasn’t invented by Zionists of course, but it was Zionists’ central argument in favor of Jewish sovereignty and self-determination in the Land of Israel as a response to murderous European and Russian antisemitism.

The Bolsheviks rejected the Zionist conception of Jews as a single people—or nation—transcending the countries in which they lived.

Stalin offered the theoretical case in his 1913 article “Marxism and the National Question.” In it, he argued that Jews scattered across different countries didn’t have a shared territory, language, culture, and economic activity and therefore did not constitute a single nation.

But I believe that the real reason for their opposition to this idea had to do with practical politics. The Bolsheviks needed the support of the Russian Empire’s vast and oppressed Jewish population, and Zionists were competition. (So was the Bund, by the way.)

The solution they proposed was for Jews to join the socialist revolution and dissolve into the great new Soviet socialist society — in other words, to assimilate. Antisemitism, they argued, would automatically disappear under socialism, and so Jews would live happily ever after as ordinary Soviet citizens, ultimately leaving their Jewishness behind. This basic philosophy persisted as the years went on. (Antisemitism, of course, didn’t disappear with the dawning of socialism.)

In the late 1960s, the USSR acquired a new reason to reject Jewish peoplehood: the dissident Jewish movement — the Refuseniks — which demanded the right for Soviet Jews to rejoin the Jewish people in their ancestral homeland. With Jews around the world staging a massive campaign to support the Refuseniks under the slogan “Let My People Go,” Soviet propaganda invested massive resources in arguing that Jews didn’t constitute a single people; that American, Israeli, and Soviet Jews had nothing to do with one another; and that Jews belonged in the countries they lived in.

This became a crucial part of the massive Soviet international antizionist propaganda campaign, unleashed in the wake of the Six Day War. It was geared first and foremost toward the global left. The latter adopted this idea along with everything else Moscow sold them on the subject of Jews, Zionism, and Israel. (See my pinned threads for my writings on the subject.)

The Soviets had an additional geopolitical reason to keep denying Jewish peoplehood: the position of their Arab allies, including the PLO. For them, the denial of Jewish peoplehood was key to stemming the inflow of Jewish immigration to Israel and denying Israel’s right to exist.

The 1968 PLO Charter declared that Judaism is a religion rather than an independent nationality; that Jews do not constitute a single nation with an identity of their own; and that “they are citizens of the states to which they belong” — a position that almost exactly mirrors the Soviet one. 

In my view, the denial of Jewish peoplehood is one of those fundamental aspects of leftwing antizionist beliefs that comes with being a card-carrying leftist. It happens to fit neatly into the currently fashionable iteration of the oppressor/oppressed binary (itself an outgrowth of the classical Marxist view of the world), but the latter largely confirms a preexisting belief. The foundations for this belief were laid much, much earlier.

text:
Jesus, I've never seen an interview like this! 🤯
Watch the whole thing or at least read my notes:

1. Yaniv was sitting in Row 11, not Business Class. He heard a woman up front yelling “Stabbings!" (She didn't say who.) Yaniv immediately stands up to see what's going on.

2. Wife & daughters are sitting around him. Then the plane starts shaking. Plane rolls very sharply leftward and back to horizontal in a terrifying way.

3. It hits him that the commotion isn't a fight in Business Class, it's happening in the cockpit.

4. He yells “Buckle up!” and runs toward the cockpit. He's 6 feet away from the cockpit when the plane suddenly nosedives.

5. It felt like it nosedived for an eternity. (In reality about 30 seconds at 30,000ft/min, reaching speeds of about Mach 0.96. Those 30 seconds of nosediving cut the plane's altitude in half.)

6. “I was flying.” He was blown around upward, sideways, he was pressed against the floor extremely hard. (A 180lb man would effectively have 540lb of downward force on their body as the first nosedive leveled out.)

7. “I kept trying my hardest to get up off the ground. At some point, I was finally able to, when the plane leveled off a little.” He speculates that a system kicked in to automatically stabilize the plane.

8. He goes to the cockpit door and there's a crew member in a white shirt, who looks like he's also a pilot. He's grabbing the cockpit door with both hands, with his body leaning down. I didn't know if he was trying to open the door, or trying to hold the door closed!

9. “I get to him, I move him away, he doesn't resist. I open the cockpit door — it was a little difficult because the pilot was lying down on the floor behind it, the one who was attacked.”

10. “I went in. The terrorist was crouching with his knees on the instruments between the two pilots' seats. There was no one in the pilots' seats. He was hitting the instrument panel, trying to break the equipment.”

11. Yaniv yells “Come help!” to any other Israelis who are also in the aisle. He doesn't know how many there are because his back is to them.

12. Yaniv immediately grabs the terrorist by the throat and starts moving him away from the controls. The terrorist resisted, but Yaniv's struggle to get him out of the cockpit only took a few seconds.

13. A handful of men who'd already gotten up from their seats together with Yaniv were already standing in the aisle dividing up responsibilities among themselves. They take over subduing the terrorist.

14. Yaniv turns back to the cockpit controls. At this point, the plane isn't nosediving, but it's still angled downward. He looks out the windshield and sees ground in the distance.

14. He leans over the pilot's seat, grabs the yoke and pulls it upward. He feels the nose of the plane come up.

15. A few seconds later, a pilot (not an Israeli) comes up behind him and says “Release the controls, I'll take it.”

16. Yaniv wasn't sure whether the other pilot was trustworthy, but he said “ok” and let him sit down at the controls. He intended to supervise the new pilot.

17. Yaniv turns around and briefly helps the men who are dealing the terrorist blows to subdue him, since apparently the terrorist is still resisting. Eventually the terrorist stops resisting, he possibly gets knocked unconscious, and the men tie him up with headphone cables.

18. Yaniv also helps the men remove the wounded Indian pilot from the cockpit. Then he goes to close the cockpit door with himself and the replacement pilot inside.

19. At this point, a member of the flight crew arrives at the cockpit door and wants to come in. Yaniv asks the replacement pilot whether to let the crew member in. He says yes, he's with us.

20. The flight crew member comes in. He has a tablet with a map. Yaniv closes the cockpit door with the three of them inside. He latches it.

21. Now Yaniv is focused on checking that the replacement pilot and the crew member are acting properly to land the plane. He sees that the pilot is talking on the radio to ground control. It sounds good to Yaniv, even though he doesn't speak much English. Yaniv can tell he's reporting that there are injured people, that we're heading in a certain direction, and that he's requesting help.

22. Some of the other Israelis were assigned to guard the rest of the flight crew. At this point, they feared that the whole crew could be conspiring. This is why the entirety of the stressful incident was about 40 minutes long. They couldn't relax until they landed and the flight crew got off the plane.

23. When they landed, one of the Israelis on the plane bought eSIM cards with a data package for everyone. As soon as they get reception, he gets a bunch of messages with pictures of himself on international news.

24. The landing was an incredible celebration. Singing, what fun we were having.

25. Let's rewind. You wake up in the morning before getting on this flight. Did something prepare you for this engagement? Something in the army? Some instinct? “Well, in the army, I was working the closest to the fire in the kitchen. (I wasn't a cook, I'd, you know, get the food and divide it up.)”

26. Yaniv personally didn't feel scared to board the second FlyDubai flight they sent. What are the odds lightning would strike twice? “Even being in this situation once was like winning the lottery.”

27. Did FlyDubai offer some kind of compensation for the incident? Did they contact you at all? “Nothing.”

28. Will you fly again? “Fly again? Sure.”

29. When are you going back to work? “I want to on Sunday.”

What an interview. Makes me proud to be Israeli.

text:
This is the true story about:
"The Disappearance of Brian Shaffer"
On the night of March 31, 2006, 27-year-old Ohio State University medical student Brian Shaffer went out with friends to celebrate the start of spring break in Columbus, Ohio.
Around 1:30 AM, they arrived at the Ugly Tuna Saloona, a popular bar located on the second floor of a building near the OSU campus. Security footage from the bar’s entrance captured Brian on the escalator heading upstairs, chatting with friends, & hanging out near the bar entrance around 1:55 AM.
Shortly before the bar closed at 2:00 AM, Brian separated from his friends. They waited for him outside, assuming he had walked home or stayed inside to talk to someone. He never came out.
When Brian failed to show up for a planned flight to Miami with his girlfriend two days later, he was reported missing. Police immediately reviewed all security camera footage from the Ugly Tuna Saloona.
Because the building was under construction, the bar had only one main entrance and exit accessible to patrons, which was monitored 24/7 by a high-definition pan-tilt-zoom camera. Investigators carefully analyzed footage of every single person who entered and exited the bar that night:
They counted every individual who walked up the escalator into the bar.
They matched each person as they walked back down the exit.
Every single person who entered the bar was accounted for leaving except Brian Shaffer.
Police checked the emergency exits, service elevators, & the construction area. None of them offered a plausible unrecorded escape route without triggering alarms or being caught by nearby municipal cameras. Search dogs tracked his scent to the exit of the bar, but it vanished right at the door.
In the weeks & months following his disappearance, investigators searched the surrounding neighborhood, rivers, & even sewer systems, finding no trace of Brian. His cell phone remained active for months, pinging a tower in Hilliard, Ohio, 14 miles away, but no calls were ever connected or answered.
Tragically, 2 years later, Brian’s father, Randy Shaffer, was killed in a freak storm when a heavy tree branch blew down during a neighborhood storm, leaving the family without answers.
To this day, Columbus police maintain an open case on Brian Shaffer.
He literally vanished into thin air from inside a crowded, monitored bar, leaving behind a complete mystery that continues to baffle forensic investigators & true-crime researchers worldwide.

text:
The Famine of the Great Leap Forward was caused by Mao's pride after the Soviet split. He wanted to pay off all loans from the USSR in 5 years instead of 16 years. All weapons and industrial equipment that USSR gave to China were loans and not gift. China had to pay compensation to USSR for terminating early the lease for South Manchurian Railway and Port Arthur (USSR's only warm water port in Dalian). As China had no hard currency like the USD to payoff the loan it had to export most of its agricultural and steel surplus to the USSR. 

Summary of the deadliest mechanics of the Great Chinese Famine (1959–1961). The catastrophe was not caused by a single mistake, but by a deadly feedback loop where political terror, inflated statistics, ideological pride, and forced debt repayments reinforced one another.

See table image attached below.

1. The Dynamic of "Faked Harvest Reports" (Wind of Exaggeration)
Under the political pressure of the Great Leap Forward, local provincial and commune cadres were terrified of being purged as "rightists" or anti-revolutionaries if they failed to meet impossible agricultural quotas.

The  Competition of Lies: Cadres engaged in frantic competition, reporting "bumper harvests" where wheat and rice yields were artificially  inflated by 200%, 300%, or even 500%.

The Requisition Trap: The central government calculated state grain procurements based on these fictional reports. When Beijing ordered      the state to take its standard percentage (e.g., 30%), it was taking 30%  of an imaginary giant number. In reality, that percentage amounted      to 80% to 100% of the actual physical grain harvested, leaving      peasants with nothing to survive on.

2. Mao's "Surplus" Illusion Meets National Pride
In 1958 and early 1959, because of these faked reports, Mao and the Politburo genuinely believed China had produced so much food that Mao famously pondered in public speeches: "What are we going to do with all this excess grain?"

When relations with the Soviet Union fractured in 1960, Mao's response was governed by fierce geopolitical pride:

Refusing to Show Vulnerability: Rather than admitting economic distress or requesting debt relief from Nikita Khrushchev, Mao declared at the   Beidaihe Conference (July 1960) that China would "tighten its  belt" (ya zhengqi) and pay off the entirety of its ~1.4  billion ruble debt to the USSR in 5 years instead of 16.

Rejecting  Soviet Offers: When the Soviets realized the severity of the famine in  1961 and offered a loan of 1 million tons of grain and 500,000 tons of  Cuban sugar, the Chinese leadership turned down the grain offer to      maintain ideological superiority, accepting only the sugar.

3. The Human Toll at the Village Level
To meet the accelerated debt timeline, specialized foreign trade teams were sent into the countryside to enforce grain collection:

State   agents confiscated seed grain (meant for the next planting season) and  feed grain, sealing local communal granaries under armed guard.

Millions  of tons of grain, soybeans, pork, and canned goods were trucked directly      to rail hubs and shipped across the Soviet border to clear the debt      ledger.

Peasants   were forbidden from leaving their villages to search for food under strict  household registration (hukou) controls, leading to mass starvation      across provinces like Anhui, Henan, Sichuan, and Gansu.

Summary
The famine was fundamentally a man-made distribution and political policy disaster. Falsified local reports led Beijing to overestimate China's food supply, and Mao’s determination to prove China's independence from Moscow led him to export actual food reserves during the peak of a domestic starvation crisis.

China succeeded in clearing its debt to the Soviet Union ahead of schedule by 1965, but at the cost of an estimated 30 to 45 million human lives.

So in Deng-era, alot of efforts were placed in auditing of information submitted by provincial cadres that they have met their KPIs. Remember they had no internet during Mao's era so everything had to be tabulated by hand and then sent via telegram to Beijing. Mao is the peasant emperor - he is not very sophisticated in the use of modern information technology and auditing techniques.

text:
Digger Rockwell is an aging oil magnate who colludes with U.S. President Compson to allow Rockwell United to extract oil in Alaska and Greenland. After repeatedly ignoring methane beneath the Greenland field, Digger learns that an explosion has dislodged an ice shelf the size of Maryland, sending it towards Europe. Environmental safety chief Dr. Nirav Ganesh warns that its collision with Norway in three days will cause massive tidal waves across the North Sea. Compson and Digger instead establish an information firewall, gambling on the slight possibility that the shelf will drift into the Atlantic and melt. The two discuss Compson's failing health due to rectal cancer.

An interruption brought by a prop failure reveals that Digger is actually Curtis Markson, the lead actor in Fossil Fools, a satirical stage play about the historic oil tycoon, and that what has been seen is the dress rehearsal before the premiere. During pauses between scenes, Curtis learns that his daughter was aboard a plane from Jamaica that disappeared after encountering a hurricane. One of the producers, Kenny, offers to locate her using his private intelligence network.

Back in the rehearsal, the shelf strikes Europe, flooding major Northern European cities. The United States and Rockwell United are summoned before the European Parliament, with Vice President Eddie standing in for Compson, who is undergoing surgery for colon cancer, where he promises American support for Europe. Digger claims responsibility for the disaster but claims neither he nor his company can be blamed for the world's dependence on oil. Afterwards, a now-drunk Ganesh tells Digger that an even larger ice shelf has broken away from a Russian glacier and is heading towards Alaska.

Digger and Ganesh inform the recovering Compson, who becomes delusional and proposes launching nuclear weapons at China. Military Chief of Staff Fitzgerald instead suggests using the weapons against the ice shelf. Ganesh objects that the attack will merely fragment it without slowing its progress, but Compson publicly authorizes the strike. Ganesh's prediction proves correct.

Meanwhile, Curtis becomes increasingly disturbed by the play's satirical treatment of events and eventually has a meltdown during rehearsal, accusing it of misrepresenting real events and trivializing the suffering of generations affected by those responsible. Kenny reveals that he is Digger's nephew and bought the rights to Fossil Fools and cast Curtis as Digger so that the public could mourn their losses through comedy. He persuades Curtis to complete the rehearsal and perform the premiere.

text:
On September 9, the Michigan Supreme Court unanimously ruled that the state can't apply its current registry law to people whose offenses happened before July 1, 2011. The state police then removed more than 20,000 people from the public registry, which had about 43,000 people on it at the time of the ruling.

What the court decided
The case is People v. Eddie Lee Smith. The court found that applying the current registry requirements to people whose crimes predate 2011 violates the ban on retroactive punishment (ex post facto laws) in both the U.S. and Michigan constitutions. The key is when the crime was committed, which is why someone sentenced after 2011 for an earlier offense was still removed.

The ruling builds on two earlier decisions:
1.  2021: The court struck down retroactive application of the 2011 version of the law, which had lengthened registration periods, usually to a lifetime requirement.
2.  December 2025: In People v. Kardasz, it held that the 2021 replacement law is punishment rather than a civil regulation. That set up the question in Smith: if the registry is punishment, can it be imposed on someone who committed a crime before that punishment existed?

Smith's own crimes were in 1995 and 2010. He served his sentence and completed parole, but was still required to register under the 2021 law.

Who was removed and who wasn't
- Anyone affected has already been on the registry at least 15 years, according to the attorneys who represented Smith.
- People whose offenses happened on or after July 1, 2011, still have to comply with the current law, which usually means lifetime registration.
- Those removed are still convicted offenders. Only their registry listing and its requirements are gone.

Reaction
- Critics: Survivors, parents and prosecutors have been sharply critical. The Eaton County prosecutor's office called the decision deeply concerning, saying victims expected the registry to offer protection and awareness. One survivor said her abuser's name, address and employer disappeared from the registry, and she is organizing a rally in Lansing.
- Supporters: The ACLU of Michigan, which has challenged the registry for more than a decade, applauded the ruling and argued that Michigan's registry is unusually bloated.
- State police: Michigan State Police has stressed that it didn't make the change itself but was following the court's order.

A claim to watch out for: Posts saying Larry Nassar was removed because of this ruling are false. State police say he was never on Michigan's registry. People who don't live, work, go to school or sit in prison in Michigan have no duty to register there, and Nassar is in federal prison outside the state. The Eaton County prosecutor's office, which spread the claim, has corrected it.

What's next
Unlike after the 2021 ruling, there's no replacement law ready for this group. The court also refused to revive older versions of the registry law, which leaves any fix up to the legislature. An appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court is possible because the ruling rests partly on the federal Constitution, but legal experts consider it unlikely to succeed, since the Court declined to review a similar challenge tied to the 2021 ruling.

text:
With 30-year mortgage rates exceeding 7%, homebuyers in the Washington, D.C. area are readjusting their purchasing strategies, reducing budgets and becoming more cautious in their offers. Real estate agents point out that while high interest rates increase the burden of homeownership, the extended sales period gives buyers more negotiating leverage, and the seller-driven market of the past few years is gradually shifting.

Compass real estate agent Yannick Ince in the Washington, D.C. area stated that the biggest change in the market is that buyers have become very cautious. While many people are still actively viewing properties, compared to the peak of the seller's market in the past, buyers are no longer readily participating in bidding wars.

On the other hand, although there are a certain number of homes for sale, some homeowners, having previously secured historically low mortgage rates, are unwilling to sell their existing homes unless there is an urgent need to relocate.

Ince pointed out that many homeowners enjoy extremely low mortgage rates and therefore are not simply moving to a new home. High interest rates are also forcing some buyers to reduce their budgets; for example, a buyer who previously received pre-approval for an $800,000 loan may now be targeting homes priced around $700,000. However, while rising mortgage rates have weakened affordability, they have also created negotiation opportunities for buyers that were previously rare. Ince stated that buyers are now starting to close deals below asking prices, and sellers are more willing to offer incentives, such as covering part of the transaction costs or providing other subsidies, to facilitate the sale.

Furthermore, due to more cautious decision-making by buyers, some homes have remained on the market for significantly longer than a few years ago. Ince stated that this wait-and-see attitude among consumers is one of the most significant changes in the current housing market.

High mortgage rates and continuously rising home prices are also placing the greatest pressure on first-time homebuyers. For young buyers who lack existing home assets and must raise the down payment themselves, the barrier to homeownership is constantly increasing. To achieve their homeownership goals, some buyers are beginning to seek assistance from family members to pay the down payment or are considering purchasing homes that can accommodate multiple generations to share housing costs.

He said that the Washington D.C. housing market is gradually moving away from the traditional seller's market of the past few years, where multiple buyers competed for prices and homes sold quickly. As the market gradually adjusts, buyers in some areas now have a greater negotiating advantage.

text:
Washington Offers $44 Million for Early Career Lessons as Long-Term Evidence Remains Incomplete

Kentucky's academic standards have children studying careers in kindergarten, and Washington is now offering states $44 million to bring career lessons into more elementary schools.

The United States has no national rule on when career education starts. States and school districts decide when it begins, how employers take part, and whether students get workplace experience.

Kentucky's standards for kindergarten through third grade cover why people work, the range of occupations, the role of money and the link between a child's interests and future jobs. Schools use guest speakers and career days. Texas provides formal career-exploration coursework in middle school.

On May 7, 2026, the U.S. Department of Labor announced $44 million in competitive grants under its Career Pathways Exploration program, which is meant to help states build career exploration into K-12 schooling, elementary grades included. The figure describes the money on offer. Completed spending has not been verified.

In San Diego County, the Cajon Valley Union School District runs a framework called The Mission of Me. It has 54 career-exploration units from kindergarten through eighth grade, with projects involving industry professionals. A 2025 U.S. Department of Education publication reported that the district's chronic absenteeism fell three percentage points between the 2021-22 and 2022-23 school years. The publication does not establish that the program caused the drop.

The strongest outcome evidence comes from high schools. An MDRC randomized evaluation of more than 1,400 students found that Career Academies participants earned about 11% more a year, on average, over the eight years after expected graduation. A Labor Department analysis of 46 career-pathway evaluations found small gains in employment and short-term earnings and no meaningful longer-term earnings gains on average. Neither study examined kindergarten instruction.

About 16% of Americans ages 18 to 24 were neither working nor in school in 2024, according to a July 2026 report from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Its research found that many of them devote substantial time to caregiving and household work. A June 2026 RAND study found wide geographic differences in the rate, with lower rates in communities that have stronger social connections.

A July 2026 evidence review by Project Evident concluded that early career exploration has a strong developmental rationale. It also found that evidence tying specific activities to long-term outcomes remains incomplete.

Washington State 

OPALENE CLIMATE CHALLENGE 

Washington climate tech founders score funding as AI boom drains investor cash

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

Oct. 3, 2026

From left: Allison Arnold, co-director of the Opalene Climate Challenge; David Gory, co-founder and CEO of AirBuild; and Aina Abiodun, president and executive director of VertueLab. 

Some climate tech startups tied to the AI boom are still attracting investors, but deals are fewer overall and times are tougher for companies addressing sustainability issues that don’t align with data center needs.

Concerns about those trends inspired a one-time Washington state initiative called the Opalene Climate Challenge, which was led by the ** non-profit VertueLab. The effort announced six investments from a pool of nearly 40 applicants.

The program planned to partner with the state to secure matching dollars, but organizers realized it would take too long to raise the needed capital. Instead, they relied solely on philanthropic donors.

“The imperative was to get the money out to these climate tech startups who are doing extraordinary work but are confronting that pinch in capital,” said Allison Arnold, co-director of the Opalene Climate Challenge.

Sustainability startups that develop hardware or physical products can face a more difficult path to scale than software companies because they typically require more capital, longer development cycles and time-consuming work to manufacture, test and deploy their technologies.

The challenge aimed to fill an early-stage funding gap with recoverable grants from donor-advised funds. Successful investments will return proceeds to the donor’s fund or another designated nonprofit.

Five of the six winners are commercializing technologies developed at the University of Washington or Washington State University. Many of the startups have participated in mentoring programs such as the Cascadia Clean Tech Accelerator or UW’s CoMotion Labs Climate Tech Incubator, or received investments from the E8 angel group.

“Those entrepreneurs who have actively sought out the resources in our ecosystem have had greater success. For most companies, it takes more than just the money,” Arnold said. At the same time, she added, “money is what has been missing in our corner of the country. We don’t have the type of risk capital that’s available in places like Silicon Valley, Boston or New York.”

The winners were featured at an event Thursday at the Seattle Climate Innovation Hub. Recipients of $100,000 awards:

▪︎ Airbuild, also the winner of the $5,000 Audience Choice Award, uses microalgae to turn wastewater treatment plants into fertilizer factories

▪︎ Ocean produces low-cost, low-carbon bamboo panels for roofing and other building applications

▪︎ ZILA BioWorks offers plant-based resins and epoxies to replace high-carbon alternatives
Recipients of $25,000 awards:

▪︎ Azotera produces low-cost ammonia for energy storage and farm applications

▪︎ Climate Solutions International offers a software platform that helps government employees analyze factors such as climate resilience, cost and carbon emissions for proposed infrastructure projects

▪︎ Emerald Battery Labs builds sodium-ion batteries to replace lead-acid batteries in commercial fleets and data centers

The first round of voting in the Brazilian presidential election will take place on October 4 from 8am to 5pm Brasilia time (11:00 to 20:00 GMT)

What we're watching: At 80, leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is running in a close election for an unprecedented, non-consecutive fourth term. His biggest competition is Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro, who narrowly lost to Lula in 2022 and was convicted for plotting a coup to overturn the result.

Lula has accused the Trump administration of using tariffs and other means to interfere with Brazilian affairs. Bolsonaro has portrayed Trump as an ally, and is expected to strengthen ties with Washington if elected.

A runoff between both is expected on October 25, if neither passes 50% of votes. Sunday’s results will offer the first real measure of the candidates’ support beyond polls.

text:
THE GRAINS COMPLEX
October 3, 2026

The grain complex wrapped up September and headed into early October under seasonal harvest pressure, following sharp volatility driven by the September WASDE and the September 30 USDA Quarterly Grain Stocks report. While late August short covering pushed markets to multi month highs, active combine progress across the Corn Belt and higher than expected quarterly inventory counts triggered a corrective pull back into month end, bringing prices back down off peak levels.

MARKET OVERVIEW
The marketplace has transitioned into active fall harvest pace, crop yield verification, and early 2027 planting expectations.

Corn saw late September profit taking and inventory pressure. After probing the $5.40's following the USDA’s yield cut to 178.5 bu/acre in the September WASDE, December futures retreated to the $4.97–$5.02 range after the Quarterly Grain Stocks report showed larger than projected old crop inventories.

Soybeans held up relatively well compared to grains, though November futures pulled back from early September highs near $13.32 down to $12.78. Strong domestic crush demand and active export sales to Asian destinations helped buffer seasonal harvest pressure.

Wheat experienced heavy selling across Chicago, Kansas City, and Minneapolis through September as seasonal harvest supply, steady Russian export competition, and profit taking washed out short covering gains, pulling Chicago December wheat back down to $6.83.

FUTURES

Corn
December Corn (CZ26): $4.97 3/4
March Corn (CH27): $5.12
Overall Tone: Cautiously defensive short term under seasonal harvest weight, though tighter overall 2026/27 ending stocks provide underlying support beneath $4.90.

Key Corn Levels
Support: $4.90–$4.95
Resistance: $5.20–$5.35

Corn Market Drivers
Bullish Drivers: September WASDE yield reduction down to 178.5 bu/acre, strong domestic ethanol grind, and steady flash export bookings.

Bearish Drivers: September 30 Grain Stocks showing higher old crop carry in, rapid early harvest progress, and seasonal combine pressure.

SOYBEAN REPORT
Harvest Expansion vs. Processing Demand
Soybean futures continue to digest early harvest yield reports as high processing margins and firm export shipments counter expanding national harvest volume.

Soybean Prices
November Soybeans (SX26): $12.78 1/4
January Soybeans (SF27): $12.94 1/2
March Soybeans (SH27): $13.04 3/4

Soybean Market Drivers
Bullish Drivers: Tighter ending stocks (310 million bushels), strong NOPA crush pace, solid soybean oil values, and active export sales commitments.

Bearish Drivers: High baseline production forecast (4.53 billion bushels on a 52.8 bu/acre average yield) and expanding early South American planting progress.

Key Soybean Levels
Support: $12.65–$12.72
Resistance: $13.10–$13.25

Soybean Watch List
Regional yield feedback as harvest accelerates across the Central and Western Corn Belt
Weekly export sales inspection pace and Chinese vessel loadings
Domestic crush processing margins and vegetable oil demand
Early South American planting moisture and progress in Brazil and Argentina

WHEAT REPORT
Wheat Settles Back Post Rally
Wheat surrendered its late August gains as global trade flows and seasonal harvest availability weighed on futures across Chicago, Kansas City, and Minneapolis.

Wheat Prices

Chicago Dec Wheat (WZ26): $6.83 0/0
KC Dec Wheat (KWZ26): $6.85
Minneapolis Dec Wheat (MWEZ26): $7.15

Wheat Outlook: Momentum has turned neutral to defensive following the September pull back, though long term downside remains restricted by tight global ending stocks.

USDA WATCH

What USDA Recently Reported

Corn Yield (September WASDE): Reduced further to 178.5 bu/acre.
Soybean Yield (September WASDE): Slightly adjusted to 52.8 bu/acre.
Quarterly Grain Stocks (Sept 30): Corn stocks came in at 2.10 billion bushels, higher than trade expectations and triggering late month selling.

Upcoming USDA Reports to Watch

Weekly Crop Progress & Condition Updates (Mondays)
Weekly Export Sales Data (Thursdays)
October WASDE & Crop Production Report (October 9)
Monthly NOPA Crush Report

WEATHER CENTER

Harvest Progress and Southern Hemisphere Moisture

Harvest weather across the Midwest remains largely favorable for rapid field entry, while early planting moisture in South America is taking center stage for the 2026/27 global crop.

Regional Global Themes

U.S. Corn Belt: Clear weather windows across much of the Midwest are supporting steady combine progress, though localized dryness in the Western Plains remains monitored for winter wheat emergence.

South America: Early rains across key Brazilian growing regions are supporting initial soybean planting, keeping long term production prospects intact.

Black Sea & Europe: Logistics and export pricing out of the Black Sea continue to dictate global market competitiveness.

BASIS & CASH MARKET SIGNALS

Interior processor bids and river terminal basis levels are adjusting to rapid harvest deliveries. Commercial processors continue to hold firm bids to capture crush and ethanol margins, while country elevators manage pipeline logistics amid seasonal harvest surges.

OUTSIDE MARKET INFLUENCE
Crude Oil & Energy: Fluctuations in energy markets continue to impact biofuel margins and freight logistics.
U.S. Dollar Index: Currency valuations remain a key factor for foreign buyer purchasing power against foreign grain origins.

Global Fertilizer: Fall fertilizer application costs and supply availability remain a focus for early 2027 crop budgeting.

FUND MONEY TRACKER
Managed money funds liquidated a portion of their late August long positions following the September quarterly stocks report. Speculative positioning will remain sensitive to weekly harvest yields and October WASDE revisions.

FARMER MARKETING CORNER
Questions Producers Should Ask This Week

For Corn: With Dec corn adjusting back toward $4.98 (CZ26), do you have commercial storage or options strategies in place to manage harvest basis risk?
For Soybeans: With Nov soybeans holding near $12.78 (SX26), are target offers set to reward potential post harvest rallies?
For Wheat: Are you utilizing flexible HTAs or call options to maintain upside exposure on stored grain?

WHAT TO WATCH THIS WEEK
Bullish Triggers: October WASDE yield reductions, accelerated flash export sales, or localized harvest yield underperformance.
Bearish Indicators: Rapid harvest hedge pressure, higher than expected yield reports from central production zones, and weakening cash basis.

FORWARD OUTLOOK
Corn: Dec (CZ26) at $4.97 3/4; needs strong export demand to reclaim support above $5.15.
Soybeans: Nov (SX26) at $12.78 1/4; supported by tight domestic balance sheets and crush demand.
Wheat: Dec (WZ26) at $6.83; testing lower support levels as global trade settles.

OPINION
Harvest is in full swing, and seasonal delivery pressure is testing price floors. While larger carry in stocks cooled late August momentum, tighter overall yield baselines mean supply remains sensitive. Protect working capital floors, manage harvest logistics, and keep a close eye on incoming combine yield readings and the October WASDE update.

text:
With prices rising across the board, all-you-can-eat buffets have become even more attractive, with budget-conscious consumers eager to indulge in their favorite dishes at restaurants offering unlimited portions. However, rising prices are also impacting restaurant operating costs. How will Golden Ranch, the largest buffet chain in the U.S., survive?

According to the Wall Street Journal, Golden Ranch originally opened as a steakhouse in North Carolina in 1973, transitioning to an all-you-can-eat buffet in the late 1990s. This model lasted for many years, but revenue plummeted after the COVID-19 pandemic restricted indoor dining in 2020. Now, business has largely recovered, with some of the busiest locations even reaching $7 million in annual revenue.

Currently, Golden Ranch has approximately 350 locations across the U.S., and while its revenue has remained stable in recent years, it is now facing challenges due to rising costs of ingredients, labor, and fuel. CEO Lance Trenary stated that almost all supplier bills now include fuel costs, reflecting this year's surge in diesel prices.

Furthermore, restaurant executives and staff stated that unlimited bread, beef, and shrimp placed a significant burden on servers; the high cost of ingredients, especially record-breaking beef prices, could lead to unprofitability and even stagnation if food production wasn't closely monitored.

Golden Ranch requires each branch to carefully review every cost. Even with unlimited sirloin steak during dinner, charging only $15.99 to $18.99 per person is crucial to maintaining competitiveness. Trinley stated that this year has indeed been difficult for the company, "We're at least trying to maintain the status quo."

Trinley emphasized that customer traffic is paramount for a successful buffet, especially in expensive locations; a loss of 500 customers per week could be disastrous. To ensure profitability, Golden Ranch provides each branch with rankings of customer traffic and cost-to-revenue percentages within the overall system.

"Golden Ranch" offers an average of 150 dishes. Trinley explained that they never hide which dishes are more expensive, but they arrange the buffet accordingly, pairing high-cost and low-cost items together. For example, shrimp with hush puppies and fries, or meatloaf with potatoes, gravy, and green beans.

Trinley emphasized the importance of creativity in the menu. He added that if a dish doesn't meet customer expectations, they'll throw it away and fill their plates with other food, so maintaining deliciousness and preventing waste are key operational points.

Trinley also revealed that they compile order data down to the minute, adjusting food preparation to avoid pre-cooking or using warming equipment, thus preventing food waste. Restaurant staff also prepare about 80% of the dishes fresh at the buffet counter. Finally, they strongly recommend the drinks, which cost an extra 3.20 yuan, but because they are unlimited refills, most customers accept, thus increasing restaurant revenue.
