Pakistani fighter pilots are already on the ground in China training on 5th-generation stealth jets.

The real bottleneck isn't stealth hardware across the border—it is internal procurement inertia.

The Indian Air Force sits at just 29 active fighter squadrons against an operational requirement of 42.5. To stop the fleet from shrinking further, India must add 36 to 40 new combat aircraft every single year.

Reports indicate Pakistan is eyeing up to 40 Chinese J-35A stealth fighters. But Air Chief Marshal AP Singh cut straight through the hype at his annual briefing: buying advanced jets does not automatically win air wars.

A stealth fighter is only as deadly as its integration. Without real-time sensor linking, unified command networks, and combat data sharing, high-tech hardware becomes an expensive target.

While India awaits its indigenous AMCA stealth program, Russia has offered its Su-57 as a potential stopgap solution.

Bookmark this breakdown to track the shifting air power dynamics across Asia.

Owning top-tier hardware means nothing if your combat ecosystem cannot talk to it.

Should India buy off-the-shelf stealth jets now or wait for its home-grown AMCA program?

text:
When an injustice occurs, the journalists, historians and archivists document evidence and facts to establish a memory, with an underlying faith: that justice, action and wisdom will follow from it in time. But time in itself offers no such function on its own -- it all comes down to the individual will and effort to make wisdom and justice out of what has occurred. And what if the power imbalance is too great between the victim and the perpetrator? Accountability and enforcement of law require not only will, but also power. The realist in this situation would say: justice can come only if we accrue more power so we no longer remain victims in the future, and so we can enforce laws ourselves that all others have understood and accepted as cherished and supreme for sustained peace. (But power is a double-edged sword: the victim, if powerful and as one-sided as the perpetrator, when in a state of humiliation from the loss of dignity, is in a position with all reasons and emotions in agreement to unleash the very act that was unleashed upon it; after all, the nature of one-sidedness is such that justice for one is injustice for the other; the nature of power is such that it is vital for survival, but also carries in it temptation towards one-sidedness.)

Documentation of facts and production of history is as equally crucial as accrual of power, and both proceed from an injury; an injury precedes the act of seeking wisdom. Wisdom is earned, which we all hold to be a truism -- but what is actually earned? Injury through injustices from the imbalance of power. Which is to say: wisdom is earned through injustices. The path to wisdom, that is, more consciousness, is paved in blood from the sheer barbaric savagery, the author of which still lurks deep down in us all. Even when wisdom is earned, it is earned for a time, since it has to be earned again, which requires injuries. Where there is power, there can be no universal empathy, and where there is wisdom, there universal empathy can exist.

text:
The true centers of power in modern intelligence and geopolitical control do not belong to the high-profile agencies or the mass armies of cyber operators, but rather to an unannounced, invisible class of technical architects. These rare individuals operate at the deepest layer of computing—manipulating volatile memory, assembly code, and hardware execution spaces—holding the keys to entire national infrastructures. Because their work demands an intimate comprehension of how physical silicon translates raw electrical charges into running code, their domain is functionally opaque to bureaucratic oversight. Non-technical administrators, politicians, and intelligence directors simply lack the literacy to audit or govern them, leaving state power at the mercy of a handful of elite systems engineers who silently dictate the limits of digital capability.
Recognizing the dangers of relying on an ungovernable technical elite, governments face a distinct incentive to shape their cyber workforces around psychologically adept software users rather than hardware-trained architects. From an institutional perspective, scaling an army of human-centric operators offers immediate operational utility with minimal structural risk. Training personnel to execute social engineering campaigns, clone credential portals, and manipulate human trust requires negligible technical depth and relies entirely on pre-packaged, off-the-shelf software interfaces. These operators act merely as consumers of tools, functioning as administrative agents who can be easily replaced, managed, and monitored within established state hierarchies.
This strategic pivot creates a vast disparity between the mass operators deployed on the digital frontlines and the unknown architects operating behind the scenes. While the psychological technologist is trained to trick a user into surrendering a static password or viewing an archived document, the hardware-level architect constructs or dismantle the execution spaces that allow systems to run in the first place. The former targets human error to gain access to stored data, while the latter holds the power to hijack live system logic, bypass hardware encryption, and compromise critical networks without ever needing a credential.
By prioritizing the development of software users over low-level engineers, state apparatuses maintain a controllable, high-volume workforce while remaining fundamentally reliant on a shadowy technical core. This dynamic leaves global economics, national defense, and international statecraft deeply asymmetric. The operators staff the public-facing apparatus of digital warfare, but the ultimate authority rests with the few unseen architects who understand the machine at its most granular level, holding an unprecedented, quietly unchecked influence over the modern world.

text:
Helen Ferguson

Regarding Helen Ferguson, the 1914 Georgia Supreme Court Record adds several serious allegations beyond her trial testimony.

Ferguson alleged a $100 bribe offer from a man, she described as Jewish, if she would leave town. 

She also alleged a separate effort involving a man who showed her attention, took her out, talked about love and marriage, and led her to believe he wanted to marry her.  Ferguson later claimed his real purpose was to pressure her into signing an affidavit favorable to Leo Frank. She said she eventually struck him in the mouth. 

Ferguson also said a foreman named Levin pressured her about the Leo Frank case. Levin’s religion or ethnicity has not been proven. A last name alone is not enough to establish either one. City directories, census records, synagogue records, or other documents would be needed to confirm it.

Why Helen Ferguson’s testimony was important to the prosecution and negative for the defense.

Ferguson’s trial testimony could support the State’s argument for premeditation.

According to contemporary newspaper reports, Ferguson said she asked Leo Frank for Mary Phagan’s wages on Friday evening, April 25, 1913. Frank refused. The Atlanta Constitution reported Ferguson saying Frank told her Mary would be at the factory Saturday and could get her money herself.

Saturday, April 26, was Confederate Memorial Day.

The National Pencil Company was closed for regular production. Frank said the factory normally employed about 170 people. Almost all of those workers would be absent. A few employees stopped in for last minute business and went during the morning for wages, and a small number of people were doing office, repair, or maintenance work.

Around noon, the factory was far emptier than on a normal workday.

Mary had also been temporarily furloughed because the sheet metal needed for her work had not arrived.

She was not returning for a normal work shift.

She was returning for $1.20 in wages, she normally earned $4.05 a week.

If Ferguson was telling the truth, Frank had an opportunity Friday to release Mary’s wages through her. Instead, he refused and reportedly spoke as if Mary herself would return Saturday to pick up the wages herself.

Mary’s unpaid wages gave her a reason to enter a largely empty factory while she was temporarily out of work.

The State used this as part of its argument for advance planning: premeditation. With nearly 170 regular employees absent, Frank had a much greater chance of being alone with Mary than he would have had on an ordinary workday.

The wages could also be seen as a form of economic leverage. Mary had money waiting for her while temporarily out of work and that would mean her earnings were deficient, that might make her more receptive for his nefarious designs. This possibility presents itself because as said above, according to Ferguson, Frank refused to release the money through her and expected Mary to return personally.

Frank A. Hooper later used Ferguson’s testimony during closing argument as part of the State’s case for premeditation.

Hugh Dorsey returned to the same point later, arguing Frank knew Mary would return for her wages and refused Ferguson’s request because he wanted Mary to appear personally at the factory.

The defense strongly disputed this interpretation.

A conflict between the Brief of Evidence and the newspapers emerged.

The Brief of Evidence and the contemporary newspaper reports do not give exactly the same account.

The Brief of Evidence was a simplified digest accepted by the defense, prosecution, and trial judge.

In the Brief, Ferguson says she asked Frank for Mary’s wages and Frank replied:

“I can’t let you have it.”

The digest then moves on.

The fuller Saturday statement does not appear there.

The Atlanta Constitution printed Ferguson’s testimony in question-and-answer form and reported her saying Frank told her Mary would be at the factory Saturday and could get her money then.

The Atlanta Journal and Atlanta Georgian also reported Ferguson’s testimony, although their wording and attribution were not identical in every detail.

The Brief of Evidence therefore contains the shorter agreed digest.

The newspapers contain fuller courtroom accounts.

The newspaper versions also contain discrepancies among themselves.

The 1914 affidavit:

Ferguson appeared again in the record in 1914.

In a sworn affidavit, she described three separate incidents involving people she said tried to influence her position in the Leo Frank case.

The $100 offer

Ferguson said an unidentified man approached her and offered her $100, plus expenses, if she would leave Atlanta.

She described the man as Jewish.

She did not identify him by name.

According to Ferguson, the offer was connected with the possibility of Frank receiving a new trial.

She refused.

The Levin incident

Ferguson also described pressure from a foreman named Levin at a furniture manufacturing plant.

She said Levin tried to influence her position in the Frank case.

Ferguson later said she became afraid of him and left the job.

Levin’s religion or ethnicity remains unverified. His surname alone does not prove either one.

The false courtship and marriage story was the final straw that broke the camel's proverbial back.

The longest part of Ferguson’s affidavit concerned Jimmie Wrenn.

Ferguson said a young man approached her in December 1913 and introduced himself under a false name: J. W. Howard.

She later learned his real name was Jimmie Wrenn.

According to Ferguson, Wrenn began showing her a great deal of attention, taking her to shows, spending money on her, talking about love, and discussing marriage.

Ferguson said she believed he wanted to marry her.

Wrenn later introduced Ferguson to another man as his supposed father.

Ferguson later identified this man as private detective C. W. Burke.

Wrenn eventually took Ferguson to an office in the Grant Building.

Ferguson remembered J. H. Porter’s name on the office door.

Burke was inside.

According to Ferguson, the men questioned her about her testimony against Frank and tried to get her to change her account involving Mary Phagan’s pay.

Ferguson said she refused and insisted her trial testimony was true.

She also said Wrenn continued talking about love and marriage while people around him were trying to obtain an affidavit from her. She likely figured out the game she had fallen for. 

Ferguson eventually discussed an earlier incident involving Jim Conley to throw the defense a chicken bone, and get out of the law office. She was incensed.

An affidavit concerning Conley was prepared.

Ferguson signed it.

She later said she signed it to satisfy the men, so it was partially made under duress. 

Afterward, Wrenn drove her home and tried to kiss her.

Ferguson said she struck him in the mouth.

She later learned “J. W. Howard” was Jimmie Wrenn and the man presented as his father "Mr. Howard,"  was none other than C. W. Burke.

Burke denied Ferguson’s accusations

Burke denied Ferguson’s account of manipulation.

He denied any effort to send her out of Atlanta.

He denied arranging a marriage of his underling Jimmie Wrenn.

He denied trying to force her to change her trial testimony.

Burke did admit one important point.

He admitted Wrenn brought Ferguson to him in J. H. Porter’s office in the Grant Building.

Corroboration:

Ferguson and Burke therefore agreed Wrenn brought her to Burke in the Grant Building.

They disagreed over why she was brought there and what Burke wanted from her.

Ferguson described deception, romantic pressure, and an effort to change her position.

Burke denied those accusations.

Three attached videos Herein:

The first lip-sync video presents the Brief of Evidence version.

It contains the simplified digest accepted for the appellate record in the form of a brief of evidence statement. It records Ferguson asking Frank for Mary’s wages and Frank refusing. The brief of evidence was ratified by the defense, prosecution and trial judge, Leonard Roan.

It does not contain the fuller Saturday statement printed in the newspapers.

The second video presents the newspaper version of Ferguson’s trial testimony.

The Atlanta Constitution, Atlanta Journal, and Atlanta Georgian preserve more detail than the Brief of Evidence. Their accounts do not match perfectly.

The third video presents Ferguson’s 1914 affidavit.

It covers the $100 offer to leave town, pressure involving Levin, and the false romance and marriage story connected with an effort to obtain an affidavit favorable to Frank.

The accompanying infographic shows two of the three incidents Ferguson described.

It does not include the Levin incident.

Helen Ferguson’s place in the case:

Ferguson was not just simply a witness who testified about a pay envelope the day before the murder.

Her testimony touched the State’s argument for premeditation and uncovered the defense's machinations post-verdict.

If her account was true, Frank refused to release Mary’s wages through Ferguson on Friday and expected Mary to appear personally on Saturday under unusual circumstances. "The spider had cast his trap."

Saturday was a holiday.

Regular production was closed.

Nearly 170 ordinary workers would be absent.

Mary had been temporarily furloughed because of the sheet-metal shortage used to make the ferrules that hold erasers to pencils. She normally during business hours used a Knurling machine to attach the two to pencils during their industrial production and process. 

Her $1.20 in unpaid wages gave her a reason to return to the factory.

The State used those facts to argue Frank expected Mary to enter a largely empty building and would have a greater chance of being alone with her.

Then, months after the trial, Ferguson swore she had been offered money to leave Atlanta, pressured by a foreman, and courted under a false name by a man she said was trying to help obtain an affidavit favorable to Frank. The defense campaign presented an attitude that it would do whatever it took to vindicate Leo Frank, and those were not the behaviors of an honest campaign trying to free a supposedly innocent man.

Burke denied her accusations of manipulation.

He still admitted the Grant Building meeting occurred.

The appellate judges could read between the lines of this manipulation and sustained the prosecution.

The Brief of Evidence, the newspaper accounts, Ferguson’s affidavit, and Burke’s denial do not tell the story in exactly the same way.

The conflicts are part of the record.

@LauraLoomer Trumps new drug factories claim about Iranian nuclear sites 

President Trump  mentioned at a rally  in Oklahoma that in fact the June 25 attack Operation Midnight Hammer by the US AirForce B2 Spirit bombers  being supported by Tinker Airforce base in Oklahoma,  was designed to obliterate  not just the nuclear reactors at the Fordrow Nuclear reactors, but also the Iranian Drug factories at the same nuclear sites 

President Donald Trump has said a lot of things about the three Iranian nuclear facilities the US attacked in Operation Midnight Hammer. Until last Thursday night, he had never before publicly claimed these facilities were also “drug factories.” 

Trump’s comments at a rally in Oklahoma bewildered not only average Americans but also experts on Iran’s nuclear program. 

One Nuclear expert said “To my knowledge, the Iranian Fordow facility, whose destruction Trump is describing, was not being used for drug production and neither had anyone previously heard any allegation by the US Intelligence community that it was.” 

The White House refused to offer any explanation for President Trump’s comments when the media inquired on Friday. 

While discussing his efforts to combat Iran, Trump spoke of the stealth bombers that attacked Iranian nuclear facilities in the June 2025 operation codenamed “Operation Midnight Hammer.” With some of the B2 Stealth planes dropping bombs aimed at Fordow’s  ventilation air shutes.

Trump at the Oklahoma rally then said, “And then at 1 o’clock in the morning with no moon, dark as can be, these unbelievable machines led by the most incredible pilots in the world, they unloaded; every single bomb which went right down air chutes into the drug factories, really. 

That’s what they were doing – they were nuclear and drug. They were doing drugs, but they were also doing creating nuclear bombs. But these drug factories-slash-nuclear factories were hit so very hard.” 

Trump has long refused to acknowledge even insignificant speaking stumbles, instead preferring to act as if instead of just amending the “drug factories” assertion, he ad-libbed three additional lines reiterating the assertion. 

The White House wouldn’t try to explain 
The White House, which tends to declare that “President Trump is right” even in response to questions about some of Trump’s most inaccurate remarks, wouldn’t offer a defense of this one. “Refer to POTUS’ comments,” a White House aide said in an unsigned Friday email. 

It is possible President Trump remembered how Iran has sometimes pointed out that legal drugs known as “radiopharmaceuticals “which are used to diagnose and treat certain medical conditions, “are produced in nuclear reactors.” 

But is well known that  the Iranian Fordow facility, Trump very much seemed to be talking about in Oklahoma at his rally, was an enrichment center with no nuclear reactor, unless of course it really was a massive illegal drug factory.

text:
Tesla is seeing a boost for its Model 3 business in Canada after Prime Minister Mark Carney’s trade agreement with China reduced the tariff on Chinese-made electric vehicles. The agreement lowered the duty from 100% to 6.1% under a quota, allowing Tesla to resume bringing Model 3 vehicles from its Shanghai factory into the Canadian market. Tesla introduced the Shanghai-built Model 3 Premium RWD at C$39,490, making it substantially cheaper than the US-built versions previously available in Canada. The new model offers about 463 kilometres of range, while Tesla also reduced the price of its Model 3 Performance. The lower-cost Chinese supply has given Tesla greater flexibility in pricing and has made the Model 3 more accessible to Canadian consumers. 

The development illustrates how changes in trade policy can quickly reshape automobile supply chains and pricing. Before the tariff agreement, Tesla had shifted Canadian Model 3 production to its Fremont facility in California after Canada imposed a 100% tariff on Chinese-made EVs. However, Canadian counter-tariffs on US vehicles subsequently increased the cost of American-built models, creating pressure on Tesla’s Canadian pricing. Carney’s agreement with Beijing opened a new route for Chinese-built EVs, with Tesla becoming one of the first major companies to take advantage of the lower tariff. The arrangement could also increase competition in Canada as other Chinese automakers seek access to the same market, while Tesla benefits from its established sales, service and charging infrastructure across the country. 

- World Business News.

text:
"People's membership in their families and home communities has diminished and their membership in the public has increased as they have become consumers, answering to the influence of the electronic media and advertising, fashions, and fads. The influence of local elders and rememberers, home folks, necessarily has decreased as the schools, indifferent to the value of local knowledge, teach the assumptions of the public economy and deference to expert opinion. Also, according to our dominant legend, the root of success, or career advancement, or the realization of one's potential as an individual, has led away from one’s orgins in family and community and into the public sphere. 

By now the rural community, the small town, even the small city, are conventionally thought to be backwards and drastically limiting of the powers, ambitions, dreams, and salaries of the college educated, who, according to the same legend, are sort of a new class predestined to success.

The public or the public sphere, centered in and ruled from the larger cities, is perceived as the sphere of self realization and success. It is perceived also as the sphere of freedom where one shakes off the burdens and constraints of local loyalties and the traditional or conventional forbiddings of religion and responsibility. 

This is surely exciting, and one can imagine how it quickens the breath of the careerist in a corporation, or a university, or a government, but, the public is not, except in the most remote and theoretical sense, a membership. It is nobody's home and its gate keepers are not filled with the spirit of welcome and hospitality. The freedom it offers is, in fact, the freedom of the richest and most most powerful to reign and the the freedom of the less rich and powerful to succeed as human resources, perhaps highly paid, perhaps not, and, like all resources under industrial rule, to be used, used up, and discarded.

The public sphere, at the present, is the realm of extremely powerful, wealthy, childish, and badly spoiled adult humans.”

~ Wendell Berry 
The Need To Be Whole,
Patriotism and the History of Prejudice

"We decided, in the language of some experts, to look on technology as a substitute for labor. Which means that we did not intend to save labor at all but to replace it and to displace the people who once supplied it… Nor did we ask the larger questions of what values we should place on people, and their work, and on the land. It appears that we abandoned ourselves, unquestioningly, to a course of technological evolution which would value the development of machines far above the development of people.”

~ Wendell Berry
Horse-drawn Tools And The Doctrine Of Labor Saving. (1978)

“The schools are no longer oriented to a cultural inheritance…
The child is not educated to return home and be of use to the place and community. He or she is educated to leave home and earn money in a provisional future that has nothing to do with place or community.”

~ Wendell Berry 
The Work Of Local Culture

An attempt to step toward a more "humane" method of execution has become anything but. From Apostle Williams
SOCIALISM HATES OUR FREEDOM
America Has Been Blessed
Many people in America hate their own country, especially African Americans who have a history of grievances against this nation.

However, if Americans could see the alternative, they would come to love this nation and what it has to offer us. Our country has never known totalitarianism, where one nation takes over or captures another and brings it into bondage. When that happens, the government totally controls people's lives.

America is blessed because of its foundation of freedoms and its constitutional Bill of Rights that come from Christianity. As a result, we have never had to experience waking up in the morning with guns pointed at our faces, forcing us out of our homes in handcuffs. This is the blessing of living in the United States, which is right now a free nation. "Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord" (Psalm 33:12).

Socialism Will Control Our Lives

This is why I often write about socialism. It is the first step to our lives being totally controlled by the government. Socialists make many promises about how their political or economic system is better for our nation. They make it sound so good, but it has never worked wherever it was tried. Socialism promises equality and happiness for everyone, but it ultimately only offers poverty and equal misery for everyone in the end.

Why? Socialism or Communism doesn't work with freedom and democracy. Instead, it is an authoritarian system in which the government controls every aspect of people's lives, including what they can say, do, make, or buy. To ensure people align with its way of life, the government must enforce it. Socialism believes everyone should live the same way. It does not support individual rights. If we do not fall in line with it and instead fight against it, history reveals they will imprison or kill those who oppose.

Socialism affects freedom by changing how society balances group needs with individual choices; it will determine our choices for us. Socialists claim it is the way to free all people from poverty, but in reality, it threatens our prosperity and our individual liberties.

The Government Does Not Produce

Socialists believe society or government must be responsible for providing people's basic needs, such as housing, healthcare, food, and education. However, the government can never fulfill these requirements. Why? The government cannot produce consumer products or offer services. This responsibility was intended for businesses in a capitalistic society. Instead, the government's only purpose is to distribute resources by allocating people's tax dollars to meet the country's overall needs.

Socialism primarily seeks to restrict and regulate business. This means at some point, the government will run out of money to provide for everyone's basic needs. That's why the government cannot afford to do this. If businesses do not provide the means of production and cannot profit, then they will have to shut down. People will lose their jobs. Now the government has to do it, but it is not a producer and will eventually run out of money.

Socialism Leads to Rationing

Consider food, for instance. If the government were responsible for feeding everyone, then food would run out and would have to be rationed among its citizens. For example, in Venezuela, people have stood in line in the streets just to buy toilet paper that had run out. Why? The government cannot produce products. Under socialism, businesses no longer own the means of production, and we end up losing the freedom to buy what we need or want.

The God of Freedom

Satan seeks to place people in bondage, which is exactly what socialism will do (Hebrews 2:14-15). However, our God is a God of freedom. He wants His people to have the freedom of choice.

And ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim LIBERTY throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof: it shall be a jubilee unto you; and ye shall return every man unto his possession, and ye shall return every man unto his family (Leviticus 25:10).

Stand fast therefore in the LIBERTY wherewith Christ hath MADE US FREE, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage...For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty... (Galatians 5:1, 13).

Now the Lord is that Spirit: and where the Spirit of the Lord is, THERE IS LIBERTY (2 Corinthians 3:17).

And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall MAKE YOU FREE... If the Son therefore shall make you FREE, ye shall be FREE indeed (John 8:32, 36).

This is true for us spiritually, emotionally, and as a nation. God desires His people to live in liberty so they can be free to worship Him. This is why God formed America - to give us freedom (Acts 17:26-27).

Rio Tinto dodges merger bullet

Rio Tinto has dodged two 'bullets' due to Glencore's rejection of a merger proposal: a possible BHP takeover bid and a dangerous acquisition. BHP looked closely at whether to bid for Rio Tinto if the latter announced a merger with Glencore. The two companies would make excellent merger partners; amongst others things, their staff and senior people have similar cultures, they are co-operating on future Australian iron ore projects and they are copper joint venture partners in Chile and the US. News/Snapshot

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

2026 Trends & Developments

Critical Minerals Push: The government has introduced a $23 billion package to support domestic processing and manufacturing of critical minerals to reduce global reliance on single-country supply chains.

Uranium Rally: Prices exceeding US$100/lb have sparked renewed interest in Australian prospects like the Kalkaroo project.

M&A Activity: Major merger talks continue between giants like Rio Tinto and Glencore as they seek to consolidate copper exposure for the EV market.

Workforce Challenges: The Minerals Council of Australia is currently calling for migration reforms to address a significant "skills crunch" in the sector.

Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic expands

The value of Alphabet’s stake in the artificial intelligence start-up Anthropic has soared to around $US124 billion ($178 billion), making it one of the most lucrative bets in the company’s history.The Google parent disclosed in a filing on Thursday (Friday AEST) that the value of its investments in unidentified private companies totalled roughly $US124.3 billion as of June 30. The filing noted that this value is “primarily” driven by one investment, which is a reference to Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified because the information is not public. The company said it recorded about $US77 billion in unrealised gains from its private investments in the second quarter, without providing further details in the filing. Google has emerged as one of Anthropic’s biggest backers over the past several years. The technology giant first invested $US3 billion in the start-up starting in 2023. Earlier this year, it agreed to invest as much as $US40 billion more, consisting of $US10 billion upfront and a potential $US30 billion in additional funding tied to operational and financial milestones through 2030.Alphabet’s filing on Thursday showed the remaining commitment has fallen to $US20 billion as of June 30 from $US30 billion at the end of the first quarter, suggesting that Google invested another $US10 billion in the start-up last quarter. Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

text:
Set Apart

In modern language, "holy" often means something religious or spiritual. But in the Bible, “holy” simply means “set apart.” It means something (or someone) different and distinct from everything else. 

God is unlike any other gods the nations knew. The Lord is holy, and called His people to be distinct—or holy—too.

Some of the distinctions that set the Israelite practices apart were religious and spiritual. They offered sacrifices in a certain way and had specific instructions for how priests, worship, and the temple operated. Other practices that set Israel apart involved everyday things like food, clothing, and their weekly calendars. These habits and customs were meant to reflect and reinforce that they were truly different—or holy—because they belonged to God.

The fourth commandment given to Israel is to "remember the Sabbath day" and keep it holy—a reminder to Israel of the blessed pattern God laid out in Creation. Just as our Holy Creator worked for six days and rested on a seventh, He calls His holy people to do the same.

What's holy about the Sabbath? It's a day set apart to be different from all the other days of the week. God intends for one day a week to look and feel different. As people who belong to Him, we can delight in His designation of some days as productive days for work and then other days set apart for reflection and refreshment.

Remember, God created special times for rest—keep those times set apart.

text:
ASIA SPLIT ON FRIDAY, AND NEW YORK SIDED WITH TAIPEI. TSMC $TSM SHOWS WHY:

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM) at $472.78, +$13.58 / +2.96% on Friday.

That is the price of TSMC's US-listed shares. The Taiwan company manufactures most of the world's most advanced chips, including the AI processors other companies design. No Asian market is open tonight: it is Sunday morning in Taipei, and Tokyo, Taipei and Hong Kong stay shut until Sunday evening, Eastern time. Their Friday closes are the last word, and they split in two. Taiwan closed at a record. Hong Kong had its worst day since March. The verdict: Asia's chip market and its interest-rate market are trading different news, TSMC's own sales say the chip side has the numbers behind it, and US futures went into the weekend on that side.

Where Asia last closed:

- Taiex (Taiwan): 48,475.74, +122.25 points / +0.25% in Friday's session, a record close, now closed.
- Hang Seng (Hong Kong): 23,972, -641 points / -2.60% in Friday's session, now closed.
- Nikkei 225 (Japan): 68,309, -647 points / -0.94% in Friday's session, now closed.
- Shanghai Composite: 3,842.19, +11.74 points / +0.31% in Wednesday's session, its latest. It has not traded since.

Hong Kong's benchmark leans on banks and insurers, and they fell hardest as the city caught up on the latest climb in US borrowing costs. It had been shut Thursday for China's National Day. The 10-year Treasury yield, what Washington pays to borrow for ten years, closed at 5.29% on Wednesday. Taipei, where TSMC alone makes up more than 40% of the market's value, did not sell on it. Tokyo gave back part of Thursday's chip-led jump, and Shanghai stays shut for the holiday until Thursday.

TSMC's numbers explain why Taipei held. In July, the company forecast its sales for the July-September quarter:

- Revenue: $44.6B-$45.8B, assuming 32 Taiwan dollars to the US dollar.
- In Taiwan dollars at that rate: about NT$1,427B-NT$1,466B.

Two of the three months are already reported:

- July: NT$467.6B.
- August: NT$514.8B, +53.3% from a year earlier, a monthly record and its first month above NT$500B.

Subtract those, and September's bar is low:

- Bottom of the forecast: about NT$445B, 13.6% less than August.
- Top of the forecast: about NT$483B, 6.1% less than August.
- September 2025, for comparison: NT$331B.

If September only matches August, the quarter comes to about $46.8B at TSMC's assumed rate. That is 2% above the top of its own range. The Taiwan dollar averaged almost exactly 32 to the US dollar over the quarter, so the conversion holds up.

Hong Kong's financial stocks sold on rising US yields. TSMC's quarter is two-thirds booked, and no yield change undoes a sale already made.

New York traded the same split after Taipei closed. TSMC's Taipei shares finished Friday at NT$2,500, -NT$10 / -0.40%. That was 1:30am ET, seven hours before the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported 29,000 jobs added in September, about a third of forecasts. The US-listed shares then rose 2.96%, to just short of their June 30 record close. US stock futures stopped at 5:00pm ET Friday:

- Nasdaq-100 futures: 31,061.75, +301 points / +0.98% since Thursday's close.
- S&P 500 futures: 7,777.25, +53.25 points / +0.69% since Thursday's close.
- Dow futures: 51,477.00, +236 points / +0.46% since Thursday's close.

The tech-heavy futures rose about twice as much as the blue-chip ones. New York sided with Taipei, and Taipei now opens on a US price that moved without it.

What would break this read: Taipei falling alongside Hong Kong when both reopen Sunday night. That would mean rising rates have reached the Asian market that most clearly ignored them on Friday. Stocks priced on years of future growth are the ones a higher Treasury yield hits hardest, and TSMC is priced that way. Moves made overnight can also fade before New York opens at 9:30am Monday.

TSMC is on none of the six Len5es. The nearest is Momentum, which looks for a stock near its high with the past month, quarter and half-year all rising. The US-listed shares:

- Since August 31: +13.8%. Since June 30: -1.0%. Since March 31: +39.9%.

What would put TSMC on the Momentum Len5: a close above $477.57, its June 30 record, which turns all three positive. At about 34 times its past year's profit, it offers none of the discount the Quality-Value Len5 waits for.

The dates, Eastern time:

- Sunday, 6:00pm: US stock futures reopen.
- Sunday, 8:00pm: Tokyo opens. 9:00pm: Taipei. 9:30pm: Hong Kong, with its trading link to mainland buyers shut until Thursday.
- Wednesday, 9:30pm: Shanghai reopens.
- Thursday, October 8, 1:30am: TSMC's September sales.
- Thursday, October 15, 2:00am: TSMC's third-quarter results and its forecast for October through December.

By October 15 the quarter is mostly settled, so the forecast is what counts. The other number is gross margin, what TSMC keeps from each sales dollar after making the chips. It forecast 65%-67% for this quarter, down from 67.7% in the April-June quarter, as it ramps its newest and smallest chipmaking process and builds factories abroad. A margin under that range would be the first sign that the AI build is costing TSMC more than it planned.

The first test comes sooner. At 9:00pm ET Sunday, Taipei opens on a TSMC whose US shares rose 2.96% after Taipei's last close.

text:
The South African GDP is 80% generated by the private sector. There is a need to ensure that 92% of entrepreneurship,business ownership ,innovation ,land and property ownership is initiated , driven and sustained by the African and Coloured commuties who remain outside of the more substantial value creation processes in RSA.

Because the private sector generates 80% of South Africa's GDP, achieving this level of meaningful economic inclusion means moving beyond basic compliance and focusing on deep value creation.

🔑 Core Strategic Pillars for Structural Transformation
To shift ownership and innovation at this scale, the economic strategy must focus on four interconnected areas:

Broadening Asset and Property Ownership
Land Reform & Property Rights:

 Accelerating urban and rural land reform by transferring state-owned land and providing secure title deeds to unlock funding.

Commercial Real Estate Access: Creating blended finance models (combining government grants with private bank loans) to help Black and Coloured industrialists acquire manufacturing and commercial property.

Unlocking Risk Capital and Funding

Early-Stage Venture Capital: Moving away from conservative debt financing. The ecosystem needs high-risk capital, equity matching, and prototype funding specifically tailored for township and rural innovators.

Supply Chain Financing: Forcing corporate supply chains to offer purchase-order financing, ensuring small businesses can fulfill large contracts without hitting cash-flow bottlenecks.

Driving Innovation and Tech Ecosystems

Decentralised Tech Hubs: Investing heavily in coding, engineering, and digital manufacturing hubs outside of traditional metros (e.g., matching the scale of Silicon Cape but rooted in townships).

Intellectual Property (IP) Incentives: Providing tax breaks and R&D grants to black-owned firms developing proprietary tech, automation, and green energy solutions.

Private Sector Integration (Beyond Compliance)
Equity Micro-Incentives:

 Shifting B-BBEE metrics from passive equity ownership transfers to active joint ventures and operational partnerships.

Market Access Guarantees: Corporate South Africa must commit to long-term off-take agreements with historical disadvantaged individuals (HDIs) to give new enterprises predictable revenue streams.

📊 Comparing Tokenistic Compliance vs. True Value Creation

To hit a 92% self-sustaining threshold, the economic model must transition from defensive compliance to offensive growth:

Focus AreaTokenistic Compliance (Current Constraints)True Value Creation (Required Shift)

Business OwnershipPassive shareholding with minimal voting power or operational control.

Majority equity coupled with executive management and strategic decision-making.

FundingOnerous commercial bank loans requiring collateral that most HDIs do not possess.

Revenue-share models, state-backed guarantees, and patient equity capital.

Innovation & IPActing as local distributors or re-sellers for multinational technologies.

Owning the patents, software code, and manufacturing processes locally.

🚀 Scalable Action Phases
Phase 1 (Years 1–3): Focus heavily on de-risking funding for African and Coloured entrepreneurs. Standardise state-backed partial credit guarantees so commercial banks aggressively fund early-stage businesses.

Phase 2 (Years 3–7): Transition into industrialisation and property acquisition. Use spatial economic zones (SEZs) to give tax exemptions to black-owned manufacturing and tech firms.

Phase 3 (Years 7–10): Focus on sustainability and global scale. Export South African innovation to the rest of the African continent via the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) framework.

text:
A synchronized green session heading into the weekend masks an ongoing structural divide between large-cap tech and small caps. In the October 2, 2026 snapshots (collected at 20:00:00 UTC), $QQQ gained 1.02% to finish at $749.58, continuing its advance well clear of its rising 20-day moving average ($727.78) with a 0.68% five-session gain. Meanwhile, IWM gained 0.90% to $281.52, but remains pinned beneath its completed 20-day moving average of $285.01 after a -0.16% five-session return.

The decisive distinction is where price sits relative to structural risk. In QQQ, buyers have an established dynamic floor beneath them, allowing swing traders to trail risk efficiently as trend expansion continues. In IWM, an oversold tick upward beneath a falling average is merely counter-trend relief until buyers prove they can reclaim broken ground. Buying small-cap catch-up bets into overhead supply offers far worse trade asymmetry than riding confirmed tech momentum above a rising moving average.

text:
An air ambulance disappeared over the Atlantic early this morning. There were six people on board.
The plane was flying from Bermuda to Boston, and the disappearance has triggered a search by air and sea in the waters off Nantucket.: “Heartbeat 104 medevac New York Center. Good evening radar contact level 240. Roger, you said you're coming in belonging. Is that what you said? OK, you declare an emergency or no? ”
Air traffic control audio posted by https://t.co/iK0dqU6sNj offered a glimpse of the flight’s final communications. The pilot’s transmission could not be heard in the recording. The controller later confirmed the pilot was declaring an emergency just before losing contact with the plane.
The Canadian-registered air ambulance jet had four crew members and two passengers aboard when it departed Bermuda’s L.F. Wade International Airport overnight for the flight to Massachusetts.
The Coast Guard said the F-A-A reported that the Gulfstream G100 had lost contact very early Saturday morning.

The Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) is the Department of the Air Force’s primary scientific research and development center and one of six centers within Air Force Materiel Command. AFRL leads the discovery, development and delivery of technologies for air, space and the multidomain. With a workforce spanning seven mission areas at more than 40 locations worldwide, AFRL conducts research ranging from basic science to advanced technology development. For more information, visit: https://t.co/kZoIqXXJK1.

MISSION
AFRL is the Department of the Air Force's (DAF) only organization wholly dedicated to leading the discovery, development and delivery of affordable warfighting technologies for our air, space and cyberspace forces.

HISTORY
The history of AFRL dates back to 1918 and was officially established in 1997 to consolidate the four former Air Force laboratories and the Air Force Office of Scientific Research. The laboratory and its predecessors have overseen more than a century of critical research efforts for the Department of War (DoW) and DAF. With technology breakthroughs found in all of today's modern aircraft and weapons systems, AFRL has contributed to significant advancements in modern communications, electronics, manufacturing, medical research and products.

PERSONNEL AND RESOURCES
AFRL employs approximately 11,000 military, civilian and contractor personnel, and manages an $8 billion portfolio of investments. The lab supports external customers and partners with industry while investing in basic research, applied research and advanced technology development. As an integrated lab, AFRL seamlessly supports the science and technology needs of two services: the Air Force and the Space Force.

text:
No, if taken alone.

Fundamentally, the War came down to differences in constitutional philosophy and interpretation that stretched back to the famous Hamilton v. Jefferson debates. Sectional differences, repeated tariff crises, the issue of Nullification, States’ Rights, the legality of secession, religion, and the role of power in western expansion all played massive roles. Slavery had a place, but not in the modern 21st-century racial-egalitarian sense in which the subject is often imagined. Southern politicians generally argued that slavery could be extended west and that the states ultimately possessed the right to determine their own domestic institutions, while much of the Free Soil movement in the North wanted the western territories preserved for free white labor. Northern racial attitudes during this period were themselves frequently extremely restrictive toward free blacks.

Thus, particularly in the territorial controversy, slavery cannot really be separated from the constitutional question of who possessed the authority to allow or prohibit it. Could Congress exclude slave property from the common territories? Could territorial governments do so? Or was the matter ultimately to be decided by the states themselves? The issue therefore became part of the older controversy over federalism, States’ Rights, sectional political power, and the nature of the Constitution itself.

Nor was the average Southern soldier simply fighting “for slavery,” any more than the average Northern soldier in 1861 was fighting for abolition. The Federal Government itself repeatedly announced that its object at the beginning of the war was preservation of the Union. Individual soldiers, North and South, fought for numerous reasons—Union, State, home, constitutional principle, patriotism, comradeship, and defense of their respective communities. Trying to reduce the motives of millions of people to one sentence does violence to the complexity of the period.

Now, the usual response at this point is, “What about the secession documents?”

But this is precisely why I think they should actually be read rather than summarized with one or two quotations. What becomes apparent is that the sectional crisis was being understood through a much larger constitutional framework. These men were debating sovereignty, compact theory, equality of the states, federal power, economic discrimination, territorial government, commerce, tariffs, navigation laws, markets, and ultimately whether a state possessed the constitutional right to withdraw from the Union.

This does not require us to pretend that every Southern state gave the same reasons, or that every Southern politician weighted every issue in the same way. They did not. But it does mean that the history becomes much more complicated once one begins reading the full documentary record.

One of the earliest examples in the Official Records comes from John A. Winston of Alabama, reporting on his mission to Louisiana on January 2, 1861. What I find interesting here is that Winston regarded Louisiana's economic position as sufficiently important that it might actually delay her movement out of the Union. He wrote:

“The State of Louisiana, from the fact that the Mississippi River flows through its extent and debouches through her borders, and that the great commercial depot of that river and its tributaries is the city of New Orleans, occupies a position somewhat more complicated than any other of the Southern States, and may present some cause of delay in the consummation and execution of the purpose of a separation from the Northwestern States and the adoption of a new political status. In consideration of these facts, more time may be required for reflection than might otherwise appear necessary, and as the convention does not assemble for some weeks, that may prevent action on the question until some time in February. As a point of policy it might be advisable for the State of Alabama to announce her intention as a foregone conclusion, a fixed fact, that on a day appointed our relations as a member of the political association known as the United States had ceased, and that Alabama, acting as a sovereign for herself in the act of separation, was prepared to form such political relations with States having a community of interest and sympathies as to them may seem just and proper. I feel assured that by such a course of respectful delay on our part other States would more promptly respond to whatever action Alabama may take, and that there is little or no doubt but that Louisiana will co-operate with the States taking action, and so add dignity and importance to the movement which is so essential to secure the respect and recognition of foreign nations and the support of hesitating States.” 

This one is admittedly not a tariff argument, nor do I present it as one. But it is important because it shows just how much commerce and geography mattered to the calculations surrounding secession. Louisiana was not situated like Alabama or Mississippi. New Orleans stood at the mouth of the great commercial artery of the Mississippi Valley, and Louisiana's economic relationship with the Northwestern states had to be considered before making such a tremendous political change.

In other words, these men were not sitting around discussing one isolated abstraction. They were thinking about rivers, markets, foreign recognition, interstate trade, political alliances, and what the economic map of North America would look like if the Union actually broke apart.

That is part of the story too.

An even more important document is the December 27, 1860 communication of S. F. Hale of Alabama to Kentucky. Hale begins his argument not with a simple declaration about one issue, but with the nature of the American federal system itself:

“The equality of all the States of this confederacy, as well as the equality of rights of all the citizens of the respective States under the Federal Constitution, is a fundamental principle in the scheme of the federal government. The union of these States under the Constitution was formed ‘to establish justice, insure domestic tranquillity, provide for the common defense, promote the general welfare, and secure the blessings of liberty to her citizens and their posterity;’ and when it is perverted to the destruction of the equality of the States, or substantially fails to accomplish these ends, it fails to achieve the purposes of its creation, and ought to be dissolved.

“The Federal Government results from a compact entered into between separate, sovereign, and independent States, called the Constitution of the United States, and amendments thereto, by which these sovereign States delegated certain specific powers to be used by that Government for the common defense and general welfare of all the States and their citizens; and when these powers are abused, or used for the destruction of the rights of any State or its citizens, each State has an equal right to judge for itself as well of the violations and infractions of that instrument as of the mode and measure of redress; and if the interest or safety of her citizens demands it, may resume the powers she had delegated without let or hindrance from the Federal Government or any other power on earth.

“Each State is bound in good faith to observe and keep on her part all the stipulations and covenants inserted for the benefit of other States in the constitutional compact (the only bond of union by which the several States are bound together), and when persistently violated by one party to the prejudice of her sister States, ceases to be obligatory on the States so aggrieved, and they may rightfully declare the compact broken, the union thereby formed dissolved, and stand upon their original rights as sovereign and independent political communities; and further, that each citizen owes his primary allegiance to the State in which he resides, and hence it is the imperative duty of the State to protect him in the enjoyment of all his constitutional rights, and see to it that they are not denied or withheld from him with impunity by any other State or government.” 

This is exactly the kind of material that gets lost when the whole controversy is reduced to a modern one-line explanation.

Hale is giving a theory of the American Union itself. In his understanding, the states were sovereign political communities that had delegated limited powers to a common agent. If that agent exceeded its delegated authority, or if other parties to the constitutional compact persistently violated their obligations, the injured state retained the ultimate right to judge the violation and determine the remedy.

One can agree or disagree with that constitutional theory. That is a separate question. The point historically is that this was the theory these men were actually arguing from.

And that theory did not originate in December 1860. It was part of a much older American constitutional debate extending backward through Calhoun and Nullification, through the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions, and ultimately into the rival constitutional traditions associated with Jefferson and Hamilton.
Hale then goes on to list the grievances which, in his view, demonstrated that the compact had been violated. Among them was this:

“During all this time the Southern States have freely conceded to the Northern States and the people of those States every right secured to them, by the Constitution, and an equal interest in the common territories of the Government; protected the lives and property of their citizens of every kind, when brought within Southern jurisdiction; enforced through their courts, when necessary, every law of Congress passed for the protection of Northern property, and submitted ever since the foundation of the Government, with scarcely a murmur, to the protection of their shipping, manufacturing, and commercial interests, by odious bounties, discriminating tariffs, and unjust navigation laws, passed by the Federal Government to the prejudice and injury of their own citizens.” 

Here is an Alabama secession commissioner, in December 1860, explicitly naming bounties, discriminating tariffs, navigation laws, manufacturing interests, commercial interests, and sectional economic prejudice as part of the history of the dispute.

That does not mean “therefore the tariff caused everything.”

That is not my argument.

My argument is that these were real pressing issues, and the primary documents prove that Southern political leaders were still talking about them during the secession crisis itself.

They did not somehow forget the tariff controversy after 1833. They remembered it as part of a larger argument about what the Federal Government was constitutionally permitted to do, which section benefited from federal economic policy, and whether one geographical majority could use national power for sectional advantage.

That distinction matters.

If the War grew out of a sectional constitutional crisis, then tariffs, navigation laws, bounties, territorial power, federal spending, state sovereignty, and the nature of the Union are not random side subjects. They are evidence of the larger disagreement about what kind of government the United States was supposed to be.
And this is exactly why I object to reducing the entire controversy to a single word.

The same point becomes still clearer in the January 7, 1861 letter of C. C. Clay Jr. to Alabama Governor Andrew B. Moore. Clay was writing during the actual process of secession. He was concerned about what would happen in Congress once representatives from the cotton states withdrew. His fear was not merely theoretical. He believed the remaining Republican majority would use federal legislative and military power against the departing states.

He wrote: “There is a manifest purpose of the Black Republicans in both houses of Congress to use the power they may have, when the Senators and Representatives of the cotton States leave here, to enact every species of legislation which hate of the South and lust of power and plunder may suggest. Bills extending the districts for the collection of revenue, so as to authorize collections on board of war vessels in view of Southern ports; increasing the tariff and making it discriminate more against the South; increasing the Army and Navy; calling for volunteers and offering them bounties in land and money; employing the militia; authorizing loans and issuing Treasury notes; indeed, every bill will be passed which they can pass and may deem necessary to strengthen the arm of Government and to enable Mr. Lincoln to enforce payment of revenue at Southern ports or to blockade them, or to commence war upon the South as soon as he is installed in office.”

This is probably one of the most interesting documents for understanding how several issues were converging at once. Clay is talking about tariff rates, discriminatory taxation, customs collection, federal revenue, expansion of the Army and Navy, blockade, and coercion—all in one paragraph. Again, I would not use this to say that Alabama seceded simply because of the tariff. Clay himself would not have said that. But neither can I read this and conclude that tariffs and federal revenue were somehow irrelevant to the approaching collision.

The connection between the economic and constitutional questions is particularly important. The issue was not merely, “How high should the tariff be?” It was also: does the Federal Government have the constitutional authority to continue collecting revenue in a state that claims to have left the Union? And what happens if it tries? Does it send revenue cutters? Does it move customs collection offshore? Does it blockade the port? Does it use the Army and Navy? At that point an old argument about political economy becomes inseparable from the constitutional question of sovereignty and the military question of coercion. That is exactly the type of chain that is lost when the whole period is read backward through a single issue.
The next document is perhaps even more explicit. J. L. M. Curry of Alabama, writing to Maryland, stated plainly that what he expected under Republican rule would “not be confined to slavery and its adjuncts.”

His actual words are worth reading: “Under Republican rule the revolution will not be confined to slavery and its adjuncts. The features of our political system which constitute its chief excellence and distinguish it from absolute governments are to be altered. The radical idea of this confederacy is the equality of the sovereign States and their voluntary assent to the constitutional compact. This, from recent indications, is to be changed, so that to a great extent power is to be centralized at Washington, Congress is to be the final judge of its powers, States are to be deprived of a reciprocity and equality of rights, and a common government, kept in being by force, will discriminate offensively and injuriously against the property of a particular geographical section.”

This is almost a direct statement of the broader constitutional argument I have been making. Curry's fear is centralization. He believed the fundamental character of the Union was being changed from a voluntary federation of equal sovereign states into a consolidated national government in which Congress would become the final judge of the extent of its own powers.

That is an enormous constitutional question. He is talking about the same basic dispute that Americans had fought about for generations: Where does sovereignty ultimately reside? Are the states constituent sovereign communities, or are they subordinate political divisions of one national people? Is the Federal Government a government of delegated powers, or does it itself possess final authority to determine the limits of those powers? Those are not imaginary issues constructed after the War. They are in the documents.

Curry then moves from constitutional structure to political economy: “To unite with the seceding States is to be their peers as confederates and have an identity of interests, protection of property, and superior advantages in the contest for the markets, a monopoly of which has been enjoyed by the North. To refuse union with the seceding States is to accept inferiority, to be deprived of an outlet for surplus slaves, and to remain in a hostile Government in a hopeless minority and remediless dependence. It gives me pleasure to be the medium of communicating with you, and through you to the Legislature of Maryland when it shall be convened. I trust that between Maryland and Alabama, and other States having a homogeneous population, kindred interests, and an inviting future of agricultural, mining, mechanical, manufacturing, commercial, and political success, a union, strong as the tie of affection and lasting as the love of liberty, will soon be formed, which shall stand as a model of a free, representative, constitutional, voluntary republic.”

Again, look at the language. Markets. Agriculture. Mining. Manufacturing. Commerce. Political independence. A voluntary constitutional republic. Curry envisioned separation not merely as an escape from a present political crisis, but as the creation of an alternative economic and constitutional system.

That matters because it tells us what these people themselves thought they were arguing about. Whatever moral judgment one ultimately reaches about their society, the documentary record is considerably broader than the slogan usually offered in modern political discussion.

The most important economic material in this section of the Official Records, however, is probably Georgia's official Declaration of Causes of January 29, 1861. Georgia is especially interesting because the document itself joins the subjects together.

The declaration certainly discusses African slavery. Nobody who reads it honestly can deny that. But immediately after describing the Republican Party as antislavery, Georgia also describes the coalition surrounding that party in terms of political economy. It refers to “the scattered advocates of exploded political heresies, of condemned theories in political economy, the advocates of commercial restrictions, of protection, of special privileges, of waste and corruption in the administration of Government,” and then launches into a lengthy historical argument about sectional economics.

Georgia declared: “The material prosperity of the North was greatly dependent on the Federal Government; that of the South not at all. In the first years of the Republic the navigating, commercial, and manufacturing interests of the North began to seek profit and aggrandizement at the expense of the agricultural interests. Even the owners of fishing smacks sought and obtained bounties for pursuing their own business (which yet continue), and $500,000 is now paid them annually out of the Treasury. The navigating interests begged for protection against foreign shipbuilders and against competition in the coasting trade. Congress granted both requests, and by prohibitory acts gave an absolute monopoly of this business to each of their interests, which they enjoy without diminution to this day. Not content with these great and unjust advantages, they have sought to throw the legitimate burdens of their business as much as possible upon the public; they have succeeded in throwing the cost of light-houses, buoys, and the maintenance of their seamen upon the Treasury, and the Government now pays above $2,000,000 annually for the support of these objects.”

It continued: “These interests, in connection with the commercial and manufacturing classes, have also succeeded, by means of subventions to mail steamers and the reduction of postage, in relieving their business from the payment of about $7,000,000 annually, throwing it upon the public Treasury under the name of postal deficiency. The manufacturing interests entered into the same struggle early, and has clamored steadily for Government bounties and special favors. This interest was confined mainly to the Eastern and Middle non-slave-holding States. Wielding these great States it held great power and influence, and its demands were in full proportion to its power.”

The declaration continued further: “The manufacturers and miners wisely based their demands upon special facts and reasons rather than upon general principles, and thereby mollified much of the opposition of the opposing interest. They pleaded in their favor the infancy of their business in this country, the scarcity of labor and capital, the hostile legislation of other countries toward them, the great necessity of their fabrics in the time of war, and the necessity of high duties to pay the debt incurred in our war for independence. These reasons prevailed, and they received for many years enormous bounties by the general acquiescence of the whole country. But when these reasons ceased they were no less clamorous for Government protection, but their clamors were less heeded—the country had put the principle of protection upon trial and condemned it.”

Finally, it states: “After having enjoyed protection to the extent of from 15 to 200 per cent. upon their entire business for above thirty years, the act of 1846 was passed. It avoided sudden change, but the principle was settled, and free trade, low duties, and economy in public expenditures was the verdict of the American people. The South and the Northwestern States sustained this policy. There was but small hope of its reversal; upon the direct issue, none at all. All these classes saw this and felt it and cast about for new allies. The anti-slavery sentiment of the North offered the best chance for success. An anti-slavery party must necessarily look to the North alone for support, but a united North was now strong enough to control the Government in all of its departments, and a sectional party was therefore determined upon. Time and issues upon slavery were necessary to its completion and final triumph.”

The Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) is the Department of the Air Force’s primary scientific research and development center and one of six centers within Air Force Materiel Command. AFRL leads the discovery, development and delivery of technologies for air, space and the multidomain. With a workforce spanning seven mission areas at more than 40 locations worldwide, AFRL conducts research ranging from basic science to advanced technology development. For more information, visit: https://t.co/kZoIqXXJK1.

MISSION
AFRL is the Department of the Air Force's (DAF) only organization wholly dedicated to leading the discovery, development and delivery of affordable warfighting technologies for our air, space and cyberspace forces.

HISTORY
The history of AFRL dates back to 1918 and was officially established in 1997 to consolidate the four former Air Force laboratories and the Air Force Office of Scientific Research. The laboratory and its predecessors have overseen more than a century of critical research efforts for the Department of War (DoW) and DAF. With technology breakthroughs found in all of today's modern aircraft and weapons systems, AFRL has contributed to significant advancements in modern communications, electronics, manufacturing, medical research and products.

PERSONNEL AND RESOURCES
AFRL employs approximately 11,000 military, civilian and contractor personnel, and manages an $8 billion portfolio of investments. The lab supports external customers and partners with industry while investing in basic research, applied research and advanced technology development. As an integrated lab, AFRL seamlessly supports the science and technology needs of two services: the Air Force and the Space Force.

THE MYTH OF THE "AUTHENTIC" THAI WOMAN
Every veteran of the grid has watched this cycle play out.

A Farang gets his heart broken. He discovers that his exclusive Girlfriend Experience was actually a highly diversified portfolio. He realizes the "brother" was a sponsor from Rome, and the sudden hospital bills for the family buffalo were just micro-upsells. He is hurt, bitter, and humiliated.

But instead of packing his bags, his ego pivots. He has an epiphany: The problem wasn't me. I just picked the wrong type of girl.

He declares to anyone who will listen that he is completely done with the nightlife industry. He is now looking for a "normal" girl. An "authentic" Thai woman. Someone innocent, who works a regular job, who has never set foot in a go-go bar, and who has never even considered dating a farang. He hopes that by resetting the board and finding a civilian, the relationship will finally be honest, pure, and free of the transactional mechanics of the grid.

And where does he begin this noble quest for untouched, traditional authenticity?

Soi Buakhao.

Or he opens Tinder and sets the radius to 2 kilometers from Tree Town. It is the absolute pinnacle of farang delusion. It is the equivalent of walking into a casino to look for someone who doesn't like money.

But let's put the geography aside and look at the cold socio-economic reality. Let’s look at this genuinely "authentic" Thai woman he is searching for.

She has a regular job, maybe in an office or a bank. She is deeply embedded in her local family structure, speaks little to no English, and her social life revolves around Thai culture, Thai food, and Thai social media.

Now, ask yourself the brutal question: What exactly does a traumatized, middle-aged foreign man who doesn't speak Thai, doesn't understand her culture, and carries a massive amount of emotional baggage from the red-light district offer her?

Nothing.

An authentic, middle-class Thai woman does not need a foreign savior because she doesn't need saving. She has a Thai boyfriend or husband who understands her world, laughs at her jokes, and integrates seamlessly into her family. To her, a farang is not a romantic upgrade; he is a massive cultural and communicative liability.

But here is the punchline of the Pattaya ecosystem: The burned expat eventually finds her anyway.

He meets a girl in a quiet coffee shop, or a modest street-food stall. She wears simple clothes. She tells him she hates the bars. She looks at the ground shyly and tells him he is the very first foreigner she has ever been on a date with.

He thinks he won. He thinks he finally beat the system and found the mythical unicorn.

He didn't beat the system. The system just read his data and changed its marketing strategy.

The grid is incredibly adaptive. When the market is flooded with farangs who are traumatized by neon lights and bar fines, the supply simply adjusts. The girl he found didn't escape the industry—she just rebranded. She recognized his trauma immediately. She saw a man terrified of "bar girls," so she took off the makeup, put on a polo shirt, and sold him the exact "innocent civilian" package he was desperately looking to buy.

In Pattaya, you don't escape the transactional economy. You just move to a different marketing funnel.

text:
Happy Birthday Charlton Heston

One of Hollywood’s most prominent leading men in the 1950s, and ‘60s, the rugged Heston rose to fame for his roles in highly acclaimed biblical epics, historical dramas, and science-fiction movies. Born in 1923 in Cook County, Illinois, after his war service Heston played Mark Antony in a film adaptation of “Julius Caesar” (1950). Hal B. Wallis was impressed and offered him a contract. His breakthrough came when Cecil B. DeMille cast him as a circus manager in “The Greatest Show on Earth” (1952), which won the Oscar for Best Picture. King Vidor then used him in a steamy melodrama with Jennifer Jones, “Ruby Gentry” (1952), and he followed it with a Western “The Savage” (1952), and was Buffalo Bill in “Pony Express” (1953). His muscular stature and uncompromising appearance might have doomed him to playing the same roles indefinitely. Fortunately Cecil B. DeMille chose the actor to portray Moses in the hugely successful biblical epic “The Ten Commandments” (1956). (DeMille thought Heston bore an uncanny resemblance to Michelangelo's statue). The film became one of the greatest box office successes of all time and is the eighth-highest-grossing film adjusted for inflation. His nuanced performance was widely praised by critics and he earned his first Golden Globe nomination. Heston then appeared in the unusual Orson Welles noir, “Touch of Evil.” The work has come to be regarded as a masterpiece, despite modern criticism of Heston for playing the role of a Mexican in brown face, which was conventional at the time. After Marlon Brando and Burt Lancaster foolishly turned down the title role in “Ben-Hur” (1959), Heston accepted the part, winning the Academy Award for Best Actor, one of the unprecedented 11 Oscars the film earned. “Ben-Hur” is arguably one of the greatest pictures ever made, and the fabled chariot race and homoerotic subtext have made it a movie that repays frequent viewings. Heston next starred in the historical epic “El Cid”(1961), opposite Sophia Loren, which was a huge success, and was in a war film, “The Pigeon That Took Rome” (1962). He then appeared in the Boxer Rebellion drama “55 Days at Peking” (1963), which, though it had its moments and an excellent cast, was a box office disappointment. Heston played Michelangelo in “The Agony and the Ecstasy” (1965) opposite Rex Harrison (it was agony for any actor playing with the ghastly Rex), and in “Khartoum” (1966), co-starring Laurence Olivier, portrayed General Charles Gordon in a somewhat wooden spectacle. After a hiatus, Heston starred in the cult film “Planet of the Apes” (1968), an eloquent argument against nuclear war, which gives the lie to those who call Heston a lifelong far-right head banger. In 1970, he portrayed Mark Antony once more in another film version of Shakespeare's “Julius Caesar”; his co-stars included Jason Robards as Brutus, John Gielgud as Caesar, and Diana Rigg as Portia. In 1971, he starred in the excellent post-apocalyptic science-fiction film “The Omega Man”, which received mixed reviews. The actor recovered with a string of successes: “Soylent Green” (1973), another science fiction picture; “The Three Musketeers” (1973), and two hit disaster movies, “Earthquake” (1974), and “Airport” (1975). In 2002, Heston announced via a taped message that he had been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. Charlton Heston died on April 5, 2008, at his home in Beverly Hills, aged 84. Richard Corliss wrote in Time magazine, "From start to finish, Heston was a grand, ornery anachronism, the sinewy symbol of a time when Hollywood took itself seriously, and when heroes came from history books, not comic books. Epics like “Ben-Hur” or “El Cid” simply couldn't be made today - in part because popular culture has changed as much as political fashion. But mainly because there's no one remotely like Charlton Heston to infuse the form with his stature, fire, and guts.”
